> **(where I is the impact well; C_local is the validated local control well; E1 is the earlier era (e.g. pre-intervention baseline) and E2 is the later era (e.g. post-intervention); and μ\_{I,E} denotes the mean water-table depth at well I during era E. The outer subtraction removes whatever gap existed between impact and control before the intervention, leaving only the change in that gap --- the net hydrological effect of moving from era E1 to era E2. Because C_local has been validated in Tier 1 to track the regional mean, this difference is free of regional climatic noise and of any secondary intervention pulses that affect both wells equally.)**

-   

### []{#anchor-19}Dune Scraping Intervention Analysis

A two-tier hierarchical BACI framework was applied across five focal wells. Three wells served as scraping treatment sites --- CEH36 (central Warren, scraped April 2015), CEH18 (western boundary, scraped October 2023) and CEH21 (coastal margin, scraped October 2023) --- and two as local controls: CEH4 (central Warren, unmanipulated) and CEH22 (coastal margin, unmanipulated). A regional mean was computed as the arithmetic mean of five C3 climate control wells (CEH9, NW7, NW6, NW5, WMC2) to characterize background system-wide trends. NW8 and NW8B were excluded on the grounds of data quality.

The scraping programme extended beyond these three monitored sites. Two further slacks in the western dunes (Scrape A and Scrape B) were scraped in the same 2015 campaign as CEH36 but carry no monitoring dipwells, and three sites in the eastern dunes (CEH40, CEH41 and CEH42) were scraped earlier, in February 2013, with their dipwells first recording in July 2014 --- seventeen months after the works. None of these five provides a pre-scraping baseline, so the intervention analysis is necessarily restricted to CEH36, CEH18 and CEH21, the sites at which a before-and-after comparison is possible. The unmonitored and late-instrumented scrapes are represented in the combined spatial driver reconstruction (Section 3.8.1) but cannot be evaluated for benefit; where that reconstruction requires a per-scrape response for them, the measured CEH36 response is assumed, and this assumption is stated in the relevant figure captions.

Because the three treatment wells span different management histories, each was decomposed into site-specific eras defined by intervention dates:

-   **CEH36 and its paired control CEH4** were decomposed into three eras: Baseline (pre-April 2015); Pure Scraping (April 2015 to November 2017); Felling Pulse (December 2017 onwards), capturing the confounding influence of the plantation clearance.

-   **CEH18 and CEH21** were decomposed into three eras: Baseline (pre-December 2017); Felling Pulse (December 2017 to October 2023); After Scraping (October 2023 onwards).

Five limitations of the control wells and treatment records bear directly on interpretation and are stated here to avoid repetition in the results.

First, CEH4 is subject to two independent sources of water-table instability --- neither of which is a change in its ground surface. CEH4 lies about 90 m nearer the eroding Caernarfon Bay shore than its paired treatment well CEH36 (221 m against 313 m), so the retreating shoreline has advanced towards it and drawn its water table down across the record; separately, it carries a sustained water-table deterioration attributable to the post-2017 felling pulse, confirmed by its Tier 1 CUSUM trajectory. Because the control sits nearer the eroding shore than the treatment, this coastal-retreat drawdown bears more heavily on CEH4 than on CEH36. Net benefit estimates at CEH36 during the Pure Scraping era should be treated as upper bounds; an additional upward bias may arise from contemporaneous foredune build-up at the site contributing to a rising water table independently of the scraping intervention. Net benefit estimates at CEH18 over the After Scraping era are similarly subject to caution given CEH4\'s post-felling deterioration. The robustness of the CEH36 scraping signal is tested independently in Section 3.5.3 using a synthetic control constructed from donor wells calibrated on the pre-scraping period and by SSM forward residual analysis.

Second, CEH22 experienced accelerating water-table deterioration throughout the monitoring period --- again a water-table effect, with no change in ground surface. This deterioration has two components. A system-wide component, evident in the network-wide −β₃ analysis, is common to the regional control mean and is therefore largely removed in the BACI differencing. A local coastal-retreat component is not: CEH22 is the most coastal of the focal wells (147 m from the eroding shore, some 85 m nearer than its paired treatment CEH21), so the retreating shoreline has drawn its water table down independently of the regional trend. It is this residual local component that prevents CEH22 from serving as a stable Tier 1 baseline; net benefits are therefore not reported for CEH21, and raw Tier 2 BACI shifts are reported for completeness only.

Third, CEH18 and CEH21 were scraped in October 2023, providing only two full post-scraping summers by the end of 2025. The short post-intervention record limits the statistical power of pre- vs post-scraping comparisons at these wells and precludes any conclusion about whether the scraping benefit observed at CEH36 over a longer timeframe will be replicated at the secondary sites.

Fourth, the pre-scraping baseline length differs substantially across the focal wells: CEH4 (paired control, installed May 2006) provides 8.9 years; CEH36 (central treatment well, installed January 2011) provides 4.2 years; CEH18 (installed September 2007) provides 7.6 years pre-2015; and CEH21 (installed July 2010) provides 4.8 years pre-2015. CEH36\'s shorter pre-scraping baseline does not invalidate the analysis: the scraping methodology does not require estimation of a long-baseline parametric covariate structure (in contrast to the clearfell ANCOVA, Section 3.5.4, which estimates a cumulative-water-balance slope from pre-felling data). CUSUM, Welch\'s t-test on era means, synthetic-control calibration and SSM forward residual all operate effectively with the available pre-event window, and the robustness analysis described in Section 3.5.3 tests the resulting BACI step against three independent methods to confirm convergence.

Fifth, the scraping analysis treats the coastal-retreat drawdown of CEH4\'s water table as a confound documented in the era-by-era comparisons rather than as a covariate explicitly modelled in the BACI design. CEH4 sits approximately 221 m from the eroding south-western Caernarfon Bay shore, and the characteristic propagation timescale (L_B²Sy/(Kb), Section 5.4.3) for coastal-erosion effects to reach inland wells through the aquifer is multi-year to multi-decadal. At this distance a substantial part of the coastal-erosion propagation envelope falls within the analysis window, so the visible deterioration at CEH4 reflects both a coastal-retreat drawdown --- the integrated effect of historical retreat together with its continued propagation over the record --- and a contribution from the post-2017 felling pulse. The Tier 1 CUSUM analysis at CEH4 captures this combined drift but cannot decompose it into its component drivers; the synthetic control and SSM forward residual analyses below provide the necessary alternative counterfactuals.

1\) Paired-control BACI design and analytical sub-procedures

Four analytical procedures are applied within the paired-control BACI framework. Each addresses a distinct research question; results are cross-referenced to the relevant sub-sections of Section 4.5.

**Paired BACI and net benefit estimation.** Tier 1 CUSUM analysis evaluated each local control well against the regional mean to verify that the controls were tracking system-wide background trends consistently. Tier 2 paired CUSUM analysis differenced each treatment well against its matched local control to isolate the scraping signal from regional climatic drift. Net benefit was computed as the BACI shift in the treatment-minus-control difference between consecutive eras, as defined in Section 3.5.1. Results are presented in Section 4.5.1 (background drift) and Section 4.5.2 (paired BACI shifts).

**Scraping propagation analysis.** A separate analysis tested whether the CEH36 scraping event --- which created a topographic low acting as a local drain --- produced a detectable drawdown at wells uphill of the scraped site. Groundwater flow toward the new drain would steepen the local hydraulic gradient, lowering the water table at neighbouring wells. The displacement-formulation SSM was fitted independently to pre-scraping (start of record to March 2015) and post-scraping (April 2015 to November 2017) windows for each of 10 wells located north and north-west of CEH36, positioned along the expected groundwater flow path into the forest interior. Seven distant C3 wells (NW1, NW2, NW11, NW13, WMC4, D25, WMC2), located 850--1100 m from CEH36 and well beyond any expected scraping influence, served as BACI controls. Per-well coefficient shifts (Δβ₁, Δβ₂, Δβ₃) were corrected by subtracting the control centroid shift, isolating any scraping-specific perturbation from background climate drift. The BACI-corrected Δβ₃ was examined as a function of distance from CEH36, to see whether it diminished with distance as would be expected if the scraping drain were pulling water from the uphill aquifer. Results are presented in Section 4.5.5.

**Summer minima analysis.** The annual summer minimum depth (June--September) was computed for each of the five focal wells. For each well, the gap between the well\'s summer minimum and both the climate control centroid and the paired control summer minimum was computed annually, and the pre- vs post-scraping shift tested by Welch\'s t-test. This mirrors the methodology applied to the clearfell intervention (Section 3.5.4) and addresses the ecological question directly: does scraping improve the critical summer low that determines dune slack habitat viability? Results are presented in Section 4.5.4.

**Scenario comparison.** To contextualize the observed scraping benefit at CEH36, five alternative scenarios were computed at the same well using its own SSM coefficients and its own per-well WTF-derived specific yield. Three forestry scenarios --- clearfell, 50% thinning, and broadleaf conversion --- are hypothetical, asking what the response would be if CEH36 had pine canopy and was then managed. These apply interception and atmospheric draw perturbations from the forestry analysis (Section 3.5.4) to CEH36\'s SSM. Two climate scenarios (dry and wet) apply UKCP18 RCP8.5 2050s central estimates. The equilibrium volumetric water table change (mm water equivalent per month) was computed from the SSM equilibrium response under two forcings: annual-mean rainfall and PET, and summer (July--September) rainfall and PET. Both figures report the same volumetric quantity, so all scenarios are directly comparable; the summer figure is the equilibrium response to summer forcing and not a summer minimum, which the equilibrium framework cannot resolve. For scraping, the on-site bar is the observed paired-BACI response converted to a volumetric equivalent, and a second bar gives the modelled off-site neighbour drawdown at 100 m (with a 250 m reference line) from the drain-cone model of Section 4.11. Results are presented in Section 4.5.6. *These four sub-procedures are implemented in 09a_paired_baci.py, 09b_scraping_propagation.py, 09c_summer_minima.py and 09d_scenario_comparison.py respectively.*

2\) Era-specific β₃ analysis on the drainage residual

Beyond the per-era CUSUM and BACI shift tests, the scraping intervention may have altered the storage decay coefficient β₃ at the treatment wells. To diagnose this, a two-step procedure is applied separately at each treatment well and its paired control. The procedure isolates per-era variation in β₃ from the confounding influence of inter-era differences in climate forcing.

First, β₁ and β₂ are estimated by fitting the full displacement-formulation SSM (Section 3.4) to the complete well record. The climate forcing contribution is then removed from each monthly observation to yield a drainage residual series, representing the component of water table change attributable to head-dependent drainage after removing the estimated rainfall and evapotranspiration contributions:

$${D_{\mathit{residual}} = \Delta}h_{t}-\beta_{1}\cdot P_{t}-\beta_{2}\cdot\left( {-\mathit{PET}_{t}} \right)$$

Second, for each management era separately, the era-specific drainage coefficient is estimated by regressing this drainage residual against minus the displacement at the end of the previous month, with a constant term:

$${D_{\mathit{residual}} = -}\beta_{3}\cdot{\left( {-h_{\mathit{disp},t-1}} \right) + c + \epsilon}$$

with 95% confidence intervals computed by OLS on each era\'s data subset. Era-specific β₃ values are compared across the Baseline, Pure Scraping (or Felling Pulse) and where applicable After Scraping eras, with non-overlapping confidence intervals interpreted as evidence of an era-specific shift in drainage behaviour.

This procedure reduces the influence of differential climate forcing between eras, but does not eliminate all sources of artefact: where the water table undergoes a sustained directional shift between eras --- as occurs following both clearfell and scraping --- the h_disp,prev term itself tracks a non-stationary trajectory, and the model may interpret systematic head changes as an elevated drainage signal. Era-specific β₃ estimates should therefore be interpreted cautiously, and spatial extent is used as the primary diagnostic: changes confined to the intervention footprint are consistent with a genuine drainage response, whilst changes extending uniformly to unmanipulated control wells point to a network-wide artefact rather than an intervention effect. Results are presented in Section 4.5.3. *This procedure is implemented in 09a_paired_baci.py as part of the paired-control BACI workflow.*

3\) Robustness triangulation of the CEH36 step

The CEH36 Pure Scraping era step change is the central scraping result. Because the paired control well CEH4 is subject to two independent confounds --- a retreating-shoreline drawdown of its water table (CEH4 sits about 90 m nearer the coast than CEH36) and post-2017 felling-pulse deterioration --- the magnitude of the CEH36 step estimated by paired BACI alone may carry a CEH4-specific bias. Three independent estimation methods are applied at CEH36 to test whether the step is robust under alternative counterfactuals.

The first method is the **paired BACI** estimate itself, reported in Section 3.5.3 and presented for comparison.

The second method is a **synthetic control** estimate. A weighted composite of donor wells, drawn from the C3 climate control set and from other reference-network wells with strong pre-scraping correlation to CEH36, is constructed to match CEH36\'s pre-scraping trajectory. The donor weights are estimated on the pre-scraping period only, ensuring that the synthetic control is calibrated independently of the post-intervention data it is then used to evaluate. The scraping step is computed as the difference between observed CEH36 and the synthetic-control prediction over the Pure Scraping era.

The third method is an **SSM forward residual** estimate. The displacement-formulation SSM is fitted to the CEH36 pre-scraping record alone, and the fitted model is then forward-simulated through the Pure Scraping era using observed climate forcing as input. The simulated water table represents the predicted CEH36 trajectory in the counterfactual where no scraping had occurred. The scraping step is computed as the difference between observed and predicted CEH36 over the Pure Scraping era.

Convergence between the three methods --- paired BACI, synthetic control, and SSM forward residual --- provides evidence that the estimated step is a real intervention effect rather than an artefact of CEH4\'s own deterioration. The three estimates and their convergence are reported in Section 4.5.2. *This triangulation is implemented in 09e_robustness.py.*

### []{#anchor-20}Clearfell BACI experiment 

A five-tier hierarchical BACI experiment was conducted across 17 wells to assess the hydrological consequences of the December 2017 clearfell. The dates of the three management interventions used throughout this analysis --- the April 2015 and October 2023 dune scrapes and the December 2017 clearfell --- are the author\'s recollection, and are used here as given; config.py additionally records CEH36 as the documented April 2015 dune-scrape site. The clearfell date is corroborated independently of any written record by the dated aerial series (Section 4.6.5): the canopy texture index across the felled compartment falls from 1.235 in the frame of 22 April 2017 to 0.141 in that of 28 June 2018, while the unfelled conifer control holds at 1.007. The scrape sites are identifiable in the same imagery, so the scraping dates are bracketable in principle by the same means; the frames currently registered do not do it, because April 2015 falls inside a gap in the series between May 2012 and March 2017, and October 2023 is bracketed only between April 2021 and March 2026. Narrowing those windows would require frames not yet in the series, and a documentary cross-check against Natural Resources Wales or forestry operations records would settle them outright; both are identified as outstanding work rather than claimed here. Wells were assigned to tiers defined a priori from spatial proximity to the felled compartment and cluster membership, with all wells required to have a minimum of eight years\' pre-felling baseline to ensure stable coefficient estimation:

-   **Impact:** WMC3 (45 m from felling compartment centroid E=241210, N=363607, inside the cleared area; 8.4 years pre-felling record).

-   **Edge:** CEH31, CEH20, CEH30, CEH16 (152--229 m, adjacent to the felling boundary; 7.4--10.3 years pre-felling).

-   **Forest control:** CEH32, CEH34, CEH33, NW10, CEH2 (C4 Main Forest interior, unaffected by felling, same canopy cover; 306--428 m; 7.3--11.6 years pre-felling).

-   **Coastal control:** CEH19, CEH17 (C5 Coastal Forest; separated from C4 on the basis of a distinct β₂ regime and non-overlapping elevation range --- Section 4.2; 9.7--10.3 years pre-felling).

-   **Climate control:** CEH9, NW7, NW6, NW5, WMC2 (C3 Western Block, no forest canopy; 571--1056 m; 8.8--12.6 years pre-felling).

Wells with insufficient pre-felling baseline were excluded from the primary analysis. The candidate-well criterion adopted here was monitoring continuity from the 2010 network expansion onwards, providing a minimum of seven years of pre-felling record and at least four years of pre-scraping record before the April 2015 scraping. This baseline length is required for two reasons. First, the April 2015 scraping at CEH36 (Section 3.5.3) introduced a level shift in the BACI gap at the same date, requiring a scraping covariate in the ANCOVA (Section 3.5.4) to avoid biasing the clearfell estimate; reliable estimation of this covariate requires that included wells have monitoring data spanning both pre- and post-scraping periods so that the April 2015 step is identifiable separately from the December 2017 felling step. Second, multiple full annual cycles are needed to constrain the seasonal cycle and the cumulative water balance slope independently of the felling step. FE1, FE2 (both installed August 2015) and NW8B (July 2015) were installed after the 2010 expansion and within four months of the scraping; their entire pre-felling baseline sits within the post-scraping era. FE3 (April 2017), FE4 (November 2017) and LIS1 (November 2017) provide eight months or fewer of pre-felling record. Following general BACI guidance that pre-intervention monitoring should span sufficient years to characterize inter-annual variability and resolve overlapping perturbations (Smokorowski and Randall, 2017), these wells were excluded. CEH36 was excluded as the scraping treatment site itself: its post-scraping water table record does not represent undisturbed pre-intervention conditions.

The clearfell BACI opens its common pre-felling window in January 2011 --- the first full calendar year clear of the 2010 network installation, when every clearfell-suite well reports continuously, and the start that aligns the monthly frame with the four-zone summer panel (Section 4.6). CEH34, in the Forest control tier, came online in August 2010, one month after the other Forest control wells, so only a single hindcast month (July 2010) is needed to align it with their common start and keep the five-well Forest control centroid balanced from its earliest point. That value is estimated by donor regression from CEH9 (Climate control), fitted by ordinary least squares on their overlapping record (August 2010 to November 2017; R² = 0.91); CEH9 was chosen in preference to the more strongly correlated CEH2 because CEH9 is a Climate control well, independent of the Forest control set, whereas CEH2 is itself a Forest control member and using it would have partially double-counted its baseline contribution. Under the January-2011 window the alignment does not affect the headline BACI, since CEH34\'s observed record already spans the whole window; the hindcast (extended back over 2006--2010 for cross-version reproducibility) bears only on rows before the window. The hindcast is implemented in 10i_ceh34_hindcast.py.

The separation of controls into three counterfactual pools --- Forest, Climate and Combined --- allows the clearfell question to be asked three ways: (a) did the felled well (WMC3) diverge from unfelled C4 wells sharing the same canopy, substrate and elevation range, the most position-matched comparison; (b) did it diverge from the climate trajectory defined by unforested C3 wells in the Western Block; and (c) against a blended counterfactual pooling all 12 control wells (C4 Forest, C5 Coastal Forest and C3 Climate). The Coastal Control tier (C5: CEH19, CEH17) is not used as a primary counterfactual in the three-pool ANCOVA --- its distinct β₂ regime and non-overlapping elevation range from C4 mean it is not position-matched to the felled well --- but it appears in the Combined pool and is analysed separately as a coastal-erosion diagnostic in the summer minima and coefficient decomposition analyses (Sections 4.6.4 and 4.6.6).

The clearfell effect is quantified through three complementary analyses, presented in turn below: (i) the network structure and ANCOVA model, which estimates the felling step from the BACI gap against each counterfactual pool, with covariates for the April 2015 scraping and the east--west coastal-retreat gradient; (ii) a summer-window analysis with a climate-collinearity sensitivity variant, isolating the response in the ecologically critical low-water season; and (iii) a per-era SSM coefficient decomposition of the clearfell effect, attributing the change to the recharge, atmospheric-draw and drainage terms.

1\) Network structure and ANCOVA model

The BACI gap for each target tier (Impact, Edge) was calculated as the target centroid mean water level minus the control centroid mean, producing a monthly time series of (target − control) values for each of the three control definitions. This monthly BACI gap is distinct from the SSM displacement (Section 3.4), which is the head above the drainage datum used internally as a predictor in the SSM β₃ term; the BACI gap is the dependent variable in the clearfell ANCOVA.

To separate the intervention signal from background climate variability and from the prior scraping event, an ANCOVA-BACI model (Underwood, 1992; Gotelli & Ellison, 2004; Osenberg et al., 1994) was fitted to each monthly BACI gap series:

$${\mathit{BACI}_{\mathit{gap}} = {\alpha + \delta_{\mathit{cwb}}}}\cdot{\mathit{CWB} + \sigma}\cdot D_{\mathit{scrape}}{(t) + \phi}\cdot D_{\mathit{fell}}{(t) + \eta}\cdot{\left( {\mathit{CWB}\times D_{\mathit{fell}}} \right) + \xi}\cdot\mathit{Drift}{(t) + \epsilon}$$

where α_B is the intercept --- the mean BACI gap (target centroid minus control) over the pre-intervention baseline, when CWB = 0 and D_scrape = D_fell = 0, absorbing the constant offset between the two centroid levels rather than being an effect of interest; δ_cwb is the coefficient on CWB, the centred cumulative water balance anomaly (cumulated P − PET departure from the long-run mean), and measures the climate sensitivity of the BACI gap; σ is the coefficient on D_scrape(t), a distance-weighted scraping covariate applying an exponential decay from CEH36 with length scale L_s = 300 m, activated at the April 2015 scraping date; φ is the coefficient on D_fell(t), a step function for the December 2017 clearfell, and is the felling step of primary interest; CWB × D_fell is an interaction term (coefficient η) testing whether climate sensitivity changed after felling; and ξ is the coefficient on Drift(t), a differential-drift covariate carrying the progressive divergence between the target wells and their controls --- the drift that coastal retreat at the western margin would otherwise be attributed to φ. Which covariate is fitted is a documented choice of the analysis rather than part of the model. The published fits use the coastal design, in which Drift(t) is the fitted coastal drawdown profile evaluated at each tier\'s mean distance from the shore, differenced between target and control and multiplied by elapsed months; ξ is then the fraction of that field the contrast feels, and ξ = 1 is exactly the amplitude fitted network-wide. An easting × time form is retained as an option and, with ξ free, is the same fit re-parameterised --- identical step, p-value and AIC (Section 4.6.3). The coefficient symbols follow the same convention as the four-zone model below: δ_cwb, subscripted by its covariate, for climate sensitivity; σ for the scraping step; and φ for the felling step. Only δ_cwb carries a subscript, because it is the one symbol of the three that names more than one quantity in this report; σ and φ are defined where they are introduced.

The BACI displacement series (target centroid minus control centroid) contains several overlapping signals: the scraping step, the clearfell step, climate-driven fluctuations (absorbed by CWB), and a differential drift between target and control wells arising from the coastal margin. If that drift is not modelled the regression distributes it across whichever coefficients best reduce the residual, biasing all estimates including the clearfell step. Coastal retreat is a sustained forcing rather than a recent perturbation. The shoreline series resolves 127 m of net retreat between 1899 and 2026, at 0.64 m yr⁻¹ to 2006 and 2.32 m yr⁻¹ since. Over a forcing of that duration the diffusive reach 2√(Dt), with D = Kb/Sy ≈ 114 m² day⁻¹, exceeds the extent of the monitoring network, so the head field at the western margin is better described as quasi-steady than as a front still travelling inland. Two consequences follow. The fitted reach of about 900 m is the distance over which the rate of change still varies detectably with distance, not the extent of the influence. And no tier of the BACI design is coastal-free: the differential the covariate carries is a contrast between positions on an established gradient, not the arrival of a signal at one tier and not another. That differential is therefore expected within the observation window, and is what ξ measures. Against the Forest controls it is 1.59 ± 0.44 and against the Combined controls 1.34 ± 0.61, neither distinguishable from unity --- the contrasts feel the coastal gradient at close to the amplitude fitted independently at network scale (Section 4.6.3). The far-field controls do not follow this pattern: there ξ is −1.51 ± 0.61, rejecting unity at p \< 0.001, with the sign reversed at the largest differential in the design. Because no tier is coastal-free the far-field contrast is not a clean test of the coastal reading, but that does not account for a reversal of sign, and none is offered here. One possibility is that the forcing has not been monotonic: the shoreline series compares 1899 with 2006 as endpoints and is blind to any intermediate excursion, while a mid-century phase of progradation under the dune-stabilisation programmes described by Ranwell (1959) would register preferentially at distance, where the aquifer integrates the older forcing. Testing that requires an intermediate shoreline position and is identified as future work rather than claimed here.

An additional step term for the October 2023 re-scraping was tested in each model and retained where it improved fit (ΔAIC \< −2). The scraping distance-decay length scale was fixed at L_s = 300 m on physical grounds (Section 3.5.3); sensitivity to L_s = 200 m and L_s = 500 m was tested and reported. The inclusion of the scraping covariate is empirically motivated: a significant level shift in the BACI gap at the April 2015 scraping date was detected independently in the scraping analysis (Section 3.5.3). The propagation analysis (Section 4.5.5) found no detectable perturbation in the drainage coefficient at uphill wells; the level shift at WMC3 is nonetheless a genuine measured drawdown rather than a coincident climate signal, being reproduced at near-identical magnitude at both the April 2015 and October 2023 scrapings (Section 4.6.3). It is consistent with a head-level drawdown propagating toward the lowered scrape surface, which need not perturb a well\'s intrinsic drainage coefficient; the covariate is retained on this basis.

A non-linear extension of this model was also fitted as a sensitivity test of the climate-buffering hypothesis. The linear CWB × D_fell interaction tests whether climate sensitivity changed after felling under the assumption that the BACI gap responds linearly to cumulative water balance; a buffering effect concentrated at climate extremes would, however, be largely averaged out by a single linear slope. The extension adds a centred CWB² term and a CWB² × D_fell interaction to the Forest-control Impact and Edge specifications, allowing the post-felling climate response to take a curved form. It is fitted as a reported sensitivity variant only --- the headline clearfell step and the linear model above are unaffected --- and its results are given in Section 4.6.2.

This three-counterfactual design produces six primary ANCOVA results (three controls × two target tiers), each with its own clearfell step estimate, confidence interval, and model diagnostics. *The primary three-counterfactual ANCOVA-BACI analysis is implemented in 10a_ancova_baci.py. *

**Four-zone pooled-panel cross-check**

The three-counterfactual ANCOVA above fits the model six times --- once for each pairing of a control definition with a target tier --- and each fit has its own dependent variable, because the BACI gap is measured against a different control centroid each time. The six step estimates are consequently not directly comparable with one another: a contrast such as Impact relative to Edge cannot be read off by differencing two of them. As a cross-check in which every zone-to-zone contrast comes from a single consistent fit, a pooled-panel model was fitted alongside the principal ANCOVA.

The pooled-panel model is a single regression, fitted once to one combined dataset. Rather than analysing each zone in a separate model, the monthly water-table records of all wells in four zones are stacked into one long table --- one row per well per month --- and zone membership is carried as a categorical variable within that table. One of the four zones, the Forest control, is designated the reference level; the model then estimates how each of the other three zones behaves relative to that reference. A single fit therefore yields three felling steps at once --- C3/Warren, Edge and Impact, each expressed as a difference from the Forest control --- and because all three rest on the same baseline and the same fitted error structure, any further contrast between two zones (Impact relative to Edge, for example) follows by exact subtraction. This is the structural advantage over the six separate ANCOVAs: there, each fit has its own baseline and the steps cannot be differenced; here, one fit supplies a single internally consistent set of contrasts.

The four zones are the Forest control (the five unfelled C4 interior wells, the reference level); the Edge and Impact tiers as defined above; and a fourth zone of four open western-dune wells (CEH1, NW1, NW2, NW11), here termed C3/Warren. The C3/Warren zone is included as a second control: it lies more than 500 m from the felled compartment, on the western side away from the direction in which forest-management effects propagate, and is therefore expected to show no felling response --- a zero result there confirms the design is sound rather than constituting a finding. The Coastal control wells are excluded from this model because they carry the coastal-erosion confound.

With the Forest control as the reference zone, the fitted model is:

$${h_{\text{it}} = {\alpha + \delta_{F}}}\cdot\mathit{CWB}_{t}$$

**(1) Baseline water level, common to all zones. h_it is the monthly water-table depth at well i in month t; α_B is the grand intercept; δ_F is the climate sensitivity of the Forest reference zone to the centred cumulative water-balance anomaly CWB_t.**

** **$$\begin{matrix}
{{+ \delta_{W}}\cdot\mathit{CWB}_{t}\cdot{\mathit{Warren}_{i} + \delta_{E}}\cdot\mathit{CWB}_{t}\cdot{\mathit{Edge}_{i} + \delta_{I}}\cdot\mathit{CWB}_{t}\cdot\mathit{Impact}_{i}}
\end{matrix}$$

**(2) Zone-differential climate sensitivity. δ_W, δ_E and δ_I are the differential sensitivities of the C3/Warren, Edge and Impact zones relative to the Forest control. Warren_i, Edge_i and Impact_i are binary zone indicators --- equal to 1 if well i belongs to that zone, 0 otherwise. Only one switch is ever active for a given well; Forest control wells have all three equal to zero.**

** **$$\begin{matrix}
{{+ \sigma_{F}}\cdot\mathit{Scr}_{t}}
\end{matrix}$$**

**(3) Scraping step for the Forest control zone. Scr_t = 0 before April 2015, 1 from April 2015 onward. σ_F is the mean water-level change in the reference zone after scraping.**

** **$$\begin{matrix}
{{+ \sigma_{W}}\cdot\mathit{Scr}_{t}\cdot{\mathit{Warren}_{i} + \sigma_{E}}\cdot\mathit{Scr}_{t}\cdot{\mathit{Edge}_{i} + \sigma_{I}}\cdot\mathit{Scr}_{t}\cdot\mathit{Impact}_{i}}
\end{matrix}$$**

**(4) Additional scraping response in each non-Forest zone relative to the Forest control. The absolute scraping step in zone z is σ_F + σ_z.**

** **$$\begin{matrix}
{{+ \phi_{F}}\cdot\mathit{Post}_{t}}
\end{matrix}$$**

**(5) Clearfell step for the Forest control zone. Post_t = 0 before December 2017, 1 from December 2017 onward. φ_F is the mean water-level change in the reference zone after felling.**

** **$$\begin{matrix}
{{+ \phi_{W}}\cdot\mathit{Post}_{t}\cdot{\mathit{Warren}_{i} + \phi_{E}}\cdot\mathit{Post}_{t}\cdot{\mathit{Edge}_{i} + \phi_{I}}\cdot\mathit{Post}_{t}\cdot\mathit{Impact}_{i}}
\end{matrix}$$**

**(6) Additional clearfell response in each non-Forest zone relative to the Forest control. The absolute felling step in zone z is φ_F + φ_z. The contrast between any two non-Forest zones follows by exact subtraction: φ_z1 − φ_z2.**

** **$${+ \psi}\cdot{\left( {\mathit{Easting}_{i}\times\mathit{Time}_{t}} \right) + \mu_{i} + \epsilon_{\text{it}}}$$**

**(7) Three housekeeping terms: ψ·(Easting_i × Time_t) absorbs the easting-correlated coastal-retreat trend; μ_i is a per-well fixed effect removing time-invariant depth differences between wells; ε_it is the residual error, with standard errors clustered on the well.**

The scraping and felling indicators enter the model twice --- once as reference-zone main effects (σ_F·Scr_t and φ_F·Post_t) and once interacted with each non-reference zone indicator --- so the absolute step in any zone z is σ_F + σ_z for scraping and φ_F + φ_z for felling, and a contrast between two non-reference zones follows by exact subtraction of their interaction coefficients. The ψ·(Easting_i × Time_t) covariate absorbs the easting-correlated coastal-retreat trend identified in Section 4.8, preventing it from being attributed to the felling steps. Standard errors are clustered on the well to allow for serial correlation between repeated monthly readings at the same well.

Because each felling step is a fitted regression coefficient, its confidence interval and p-value follow directly from the OLS output. A contrast between two non-reference zones --- such as the Impact step relative to the Edge step --- is not itself a fitted coefficient but the difference of two; its point estimate is exact, but its standard error must be computed from the model\'s coefficient covariance matrix rather than by subtracting the two separate standard errors. Such derived contrasts can acquire misleadingly narrow intervals when the two zones are strongly correlated, so their p-values are not treated as independent evidence of an effect; the Impact-to-Edge contrast is instead corroborated against the separate two-zone estimator of Script 10j. This pooled-panel model tests whether the felling signal survives estimation in one jointly fitted panel; it supplements, and does not replace, the principal ANCOVA.

The same four-zone structure is also applied to the annual June--September summer-minimum series, to provide the equivalent cross-check at the summer extreme; at that resolution the scraping term is dropped. *The monthly four-zone model is implemented in 10k_four_zone_baci.py and the summer-minimum companion in 10l_four_zone_summer_minima.py.*

**Spatial step-change mapping.** The post-felling step at each reference well --- relative to its pre-felling mean and corrected by subtracting the appropriate control centroid step --- was computed and rendered as climate-corrected spatial maps for the felling and scraping eras (Figures 34 and 25). These maps provide a visual diagnostic of whether the step changes show a spatial gradient consistent with a localized intervention effect. *Spatial step-change mapping is implemented in 10b_spatial_step_maps.py*

**Within-forest position-matching.** The within-forest spatial coefficient analysis (Section 3.4.4, results in Section 4.9.4) underpins the C4-only composition of the Forest control: it establishes that elevation alone explains 97% of within-forest β₂ variance, so position-matched controls rather than canopy-matched controls are the appropriate counterfactual for testing canopy management effects. *The within-forest spatial coefficient analysis is implemented 10c_forest_zone_analysis.py.*

2\) Summer-window analysis and climate-collinearity sensitivity

The annual BACI step estimated from the ANCOVA above is computed over all monthly observations from the start of record to the analysis cutoff. Because the ecological consequences of any water table change concentrate in the summer months when slack inundation determines habitat viability, a parallel summer-window ANCOVA is fitted directly to June--September observations only, using the same model specification, control definitions, and covariates as the annual analysis. This directly-fitted summer ANCOVA provides a monthly-resolution estimate of the clearfell step over the ecologically critical period, without the seasonal scaling assumption implicit in extrapolating an annual estimate.

A sensitivity variant of the summer-window analysis is additionally fitted with the CWB covariate and the CWB × D_fell interaction dropped from the design matrix. Within the restricted June--September window, the CWB covariate covaries more closely with the clearfell step indicator than it does in the annual window, because the summer-only data captures the part of the seasonal cycle in which the climate-balance trajectory and the post-2017 felling step share the most temporal overlap. This collinearity inflates the standard error on the clearfell step coefficient in the full-specification fit and may absorb a portion of the felling signal into the CWB term. The sensitivity variant tests how much the summer step estimate depends on the CWB specification; the interpretation of the two estimates and the mechanistic argument for the collinearity behaviour are presented in Section 4.6.3.

A separate annual summer-minimum analysis is also computed. For each well in the 17-well network, the annual summer minimum depth (June--September) was computed and the gap between the well\'s summer minimum and the control centroid summer minimum was tracked annually. The pre- versus post-felling shift in this gap was tested by Welch\'s t-test, and tier-mean shifts were computed for both forest and climate control centroids. A mixed-effects model with random intercept per well and fixed effects for post-felling and post-scraping indicators was fitted to each tier to provide a pooled clearfell step estimate with proper uncertainty:

$${\mathit{gap} = {\alpha + \phi}}\cdot{D_{\mathit{fell}} + \sigma}\cdot{D_{\mathit{scrape}} + u_{\mathit{well}} + \epsilon}$$

where gap is the annual difference between the well\'s summer-minimum depth and the control-centroid summer minimum; α_B is the fixed intercept, the mean gap over the pre-felling baseline; φ is the coefficient on D_fell, the pooled clearfell step and the quantity of interest; σ is the coefficient on D_scrape, the scraping step; D_fell and D_scrape are post-intervention step indicators, equal to zero before and one from the December 2017 clearfell and April 2015 scraping dates respectively; u_well is a random intercept for each well, absorbing time-invariant between-well differences in mean gap; and ϵ is the residual error. As elsewhere in this section, φ denotes the felling step and σ the scraping step.

The directly-fitted summer ANCOVA, the CWB-dropped sensitivity, and the annual summer-minimum mixed-effects model are each reported in Section 4.6.3 to provide three complementary perspectives on the summer-specific response of the clearfell-affected wells.

*The directly-fitted summer-window ANCOVA and the CWB-dropped sensitivity variant are produced by the same script as the annual analysis (10a_ancova_baci.py); the annual summer-minimum mixed-effects model is implemented in 10d_summer_minima.py.*

3\) Per-era SSM coefficient decomposition of the clearfell effect.

The clearfell intervention may have altered the recharge, atmospheric draw and drainage responses of the affected aquifer (Komatsu et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2015). To diagnose these changes mechanistically, the SSM coefficients β₁, β₂ and β₃ are estimated separately for the pre-intervention (Before) and post-intervention (After) eras at each well in the clearfell BACI network, and the differences Δβ₁ = β₁,After − β₁,Before, Δβ₂ = β₂,After − β₂,Before and Δβ₃ = β₃,After − β₃,Before are interpreted as the recharge, atmospheric draw and drainage shifts attributable to the intervention.

Both era-specific SSMs are fitted on the displacement formulation defined in Section 3.4, so β₃ is the displacement-storage coefficient (positive, Darcy-consistent) in both eras. The Before era is the record-length-balanced pre-intervention window, with an additional binary dummy in the design matrix at wells affected by the April 2015 scraping pulse to absorb that earlier intervention. The After era extends from the intervention date to the end of record. Both fits retain an intercept term, on the grounds that the era-mean residual carries information about non-mechanistic baseline shifts (background drift, instrument offsets, large-scale climate departures from the long-term mean) that the β coefficients themselves should not be forced to absorb.

The mechanistic prediction of the intervention effect, projected onto the post-intervention climate, is then computed at each well as:

$$\Delta{h_{\mathit{predicted}} = \Delta}\beta_{1}\cdot\overline{P_{\mathit{after}}}-\Delta\beta_{2}\cdot\overline{\mathit{PET}_{\mathit{after}}}-\Delta\beta_{3}\cdot\overline{h_{\mathit{disp},\mathit{after}}}$$

where bar P_after, bar PET_after and bar h_disp,after are the post-intervention era means of rainfall, PET and displacement above the drainage datum. This expression isolates the change in the climate-driven and drainage-driven response of the aquifer from the change in baseline level, by holding the climate forcing and head position at their post-intervention values and varying only the coefficients.

Δh_predicted is compared to the observed BACI step Δh_observed estimated from the ANCOVA model in Section 3.5.4. The Δh_predicted formula captures only the β·X component of the era shift; the intercept difference Δα_B = α_After − α_Before absorbs the era-mean residual, which at most wells is the dominant component of the observed step. The predicted-versus-observed comparison is therefore informative about the mechanistic decomposition (Δβ₁ recharge, Δβ₂ atmospheric draw, Δβ₃ drainage) but should not be read as a complete reconstruction of the BACI step. The interpretation of the Δα residual --- whether it represents genuinely non-mechanistic baseline drift, mis-specification of one of the β terms, or a structural state shift not captured by the time-invariant SSM --- is taken up in Section 4.6.7.

Two additional supplementary analyses extend the mechanistic decomposition. The SSM residual normalization calibrates the SSM on the pre-felling record for each well, runs it forward iteratively using observed climate forcing, and normalizes the post-felling residuals (observed minus predicted) by subtracting the forest control mean residual; this provides a climate-independent test of clearfell-specific displacement and is presented in Section 4.6.7. A synthetic counterfactual for the Impact and Edge tiers is constructed from an optimally weighted combination of six donor wells calibrated on the pre-intervention period, with the gap between observed and synthetic post-felling providing an estimate of the intervention effect that does not rely on the ANCOVA parametric assumptions; this is also presented in Section 4.6.7. A clearfell transect analysis tests whether the post-felling response shows a spatial gradient consistent with a localized clearfell effect, comparing era-mean depths across a transect from the plantation interior to the felling core, and testing whether the broadleaf-canopy well diverges from the pine composite over time, rolling-window SSM coefficient tracking, and drainage diagnostic plots, with limitations of the NW10 broadleaf comparison discussed in Section 6.3.

A separate synthetic-extension analysis tests whether the FE1 and FE2 wells, sited inside or at the immediate edge of the clearfell compartment but excluded from the primary ANCOVA on the grounds of insufficient pre-scraping baseline, confirm the WMC3 Impact result. Their records were extended backwards using OLS donor regression onto the three Forest Control wells CEH34, CEH2, and CEH33, selected on the basis of proximity, shared canopy conditions, and pre-clearfell correlation (r \> 0.99 for both FE wells). The regression was calibrated on the pre-clearfell overlap window (July 2015 to November 2017, n = 29 months) and applied to hindcast FE well levels back to July 2010, providing a synthetic pre-scraping baseline. The synthetic hindcast was spliced with the actual FE observations to create a stable-composition impact centroid spanning all three eras (pre-scraping, post-scraping, post-felling). Three impact centroid variants were tested: (A) WMC3 + FE1 + FE2; (B) WMC3 + FE2; and (C) WMC3 alone. Each was run through the same ANCOVA framework as the primary analysis, against the Forest, Climate, and Combined control definitions. FE1 is caveated as sitting approximately 20 m outside the clearfell boundary in standing forest. Results are presented in Section 4.6.7.

*The per-era SSM coefficient decomposition is implemented in 10e_coefficient_decomposition.py. The SSM residual normalization and synthetic-control analyses are implemented in 10f_robustness.py; the transect, NW10 broadleaf trend, and rolling-window diagnostics in 10g_diagnostics.py; and the synthetic FE well extension in 10h_synthetic_impact_baci.py. Shared data loading and spatial functions are in clearfell_common.py. The clearfell BACI experiment as a whole is orchestrated by run_10_clearfell.py.*

## []{#anchor-21}Threshold Forecasting

To translate the observed spatial dynamics into predictive management tools, operational forecasting equations were derived using a multi-tiered mathematical framework. This approach combines continuous mass-balance modelling with seasonal prediction equations to quantify the aquifer\'s climatic vulnerability.

### []{#anchor-22}**Cluster-Level Mechanistic State-Space Equations** 

The cluster-level SSM coefficients derived in Section 3.4.1 were used to construct operational P_flood threshold equations for each of the five principal clusters. The model was fitted with the intercept strictly forced to zero, ensuring that the coefficients represent a strict physical mass balance and providing the basis for algebraic inversion in Section 3.6.3.

### []{#anchor-23}Seasonal Prediction Equations

While the SSM operates on a continuous monthly basis, conservation management typically requires inter-seasonal risk forecasting --- specifically, predicting winter flood peaks and summer drought minima from antecedent conditions. To address this, autoregressive prediction equations were fitted at a hydrological-year resolution for the three primary structural domains: Eastern Block, Western Block, and Forest clusters.

Two equations are fitted for each domain. The winter prediction equation predicts the peak winter water table (h_peak) from cumulative winter precipitation and the antecedent summer minimum:

$${h_{\mathit{peak}} = a}\cdot{P_{\mathit{winter}} + b}\cdot{h_{\mathit{\min}} + c}$$

The summer prediction equation predicts the summer minimum water table (h_min) from cumulative summer precipitation and the antecedent winter peak:

$${h_{\mathit{\min}} = a}\cdot{P_{\mathit{summer}} + b}\cdot{h_{\mathit{\max},\mathit{winter}} + c}$$

where P_winter is cumulative precipitation over October--March, P_summer is cumulative precipitation over April--September, h_min is the preceding summer minimum water table depth, h\_{max,winter} is the preceding winter maximum water table depth, *a* is the fitted regression coefficient on the seasonal precipitation predictor, *b* is the fitted coefficient on the antecedent-state predictor, and *c* is a fitted intercept. The seasonal equations are AR(1)-style empirical regressions at hydrological-year resolution, providing operational forecasting at coarser temporal resolution than the monthly SSM described in Section 3.4. Data are organized by hydrological year commencing 1 October.

Head-dependent drainage (the −β₃·h(t−1) term in the SSM) is not fitted as a separate parameter at the seasonal scale: with one observation per hydrological year, drainage and the antecedent-state term are aliased, so drainage is absorbed implicitly into *b* and the fitted intercept *c* rather than appearing as a separate coefficient.

The antecedent-state terms (h_min in the winter equation, h_max in the summer equation) explicitly formalize the memory of the dune aquifer system --- the degree to which a winter flood peak is conditioned by the depth of the preceding summer drought, and vice versa. This parameterization allows managers to construct simple conditional forecasts: given a known or projected winter rainfall total and the current summer water table position, the expected winter flood maximum can be estimated directly from the fitted equation without running the full SSM.

### []{#anchor-24}**Algebraic Derivation of the Critical Rainfall Threshold (P_flood​)**

The most operationally significant metric for dune slack management is the critical rainfall threshold (P_flood) --- the cumulative winter rainfall depth required to raise the water table from its summer minimum to the elevation of the slack floor (h_target, where depth to water table equals zero).

This threshold was derived by iterating the cluster-level state-space equation (Section 3.4.1) forward from the September summer minimum (h₀) over the months from October to each cluster\'s historical peak-of-record month. The horizon is therefore cluster-specific and reflects the observed timing of winter peak water table: five months (October--February) for C1 and C2, and six months (October--March) for C3, C4 and C5.

The monthly recurrence equation --- applied once per step from October to the peak month --- is:

$${h_{t} = \left( {1-\beta_{3}} \right)}\cdot{h_{t-1} + \beta_{1}}\cdot P_{t}-\beta_{2}\cdot E_{t}-\beta_{3}\cdot z_{0}$$

*(1) h_t is the water level at the end of month t. The term (1 − β₃)·h\_{t−1} is how much of last month\'s displacement survives into this month --- close to 1 for sluggish aquifers such as C4, lower for fast-draining ones such as C1. β₁·P_t is the recharge contribution from this month\'s rainfall; β₂·E_t is the atmospheric draw-down from PET; β₃·z₀ is the drainage loss proportional to the fixed datum displacement. Monthly precipitation is expressed as P_t = m_P·P̄\_t, where P̄\_t is the long-term monthly mean rainfall from the RAF Valley reference climatology and m_P is a multiplier representing the departure of a given winter from the long-term mean. Monthly PET is taken directly from the climatology (E_t = Ē_t) without scaling, reflecting the fact that winter PET varies considerably less year-to-year than winter rainfall at this latitude.*

Letting ρ_h = 1 − β₃, iterating the recurrence forward n months from h₀ yields the closed form:

$${h_{n} = h_{0}}\cdot{{\rho_{h}}^{n} + \beta_{1}}\cdot{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\rho_{h}}^{n-i}}\cdot m_{P}\cdot{\overline{P}}_{i}-\beta_{2}\cdot{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\rho_{h}}^{n-i}}\cdot{\overline{E}}_{i}-z_{0}\cdot\left( {1-{\rho_{h}}^{n}} \right)$$

*(2) h_n is the water level after n months of winter recharge. Rather than stepping through the equation n times, this single expression accumulates the effect of all n monthly steps at once. The term h₀·ρ_hⁿ is how much of the starting summer deficit survives n months of drainage --- for a C2 well with ρ_h = 0.93, roughly 71% of the September deficit persists to February. The two summation terms accumulate the rainfall benefit and PET cost month by month, with the weighting ρ_h\^{n−i} giving greater influence to earlier months because they have more remaining winter months to amplify their contribution. The final term z₀·(1−ρ_hⁿ) is the cumulative drainage loss over the horizon, where z₀ is the drainage datum defined in Section 3.4.1 --- a fixed reference depth of 3.7 m below ground surface, not the hydraulic diffusivity that carries the same letter elsewhere in the literature.*

Setting h_n = h_target and solving for m_P:

$$m_{P} = \frac{h_{\mathit{target}}-h_{0}\cdot{{\rho_{h}}^{n} + \beta_{2}}\cdot{S_{E} + z_{0}}\cdot\left( {1-{\rho_{h}}^{n}} \right)}{\beta_{1}\cdot S_{P}}$$

*(3) m_P is the rainfall multiplier needed to raise the water table to the slack floor from a given summer minimum h₀. The numerator is everything the aquifer must overcome: the slack-floor target level (h_target), the starting deficit (−h₀·ρ_hⁿ), the cumulative PET demand (β₂·S_E), and the drainage losses (z₀·(1−ρ_hⁿ)). The denominator is the drainage-weighted rainfall the winter can supply at climatological rates (β₁·S_P). Here S_P = Σρ_h\^{n−i}·P̄\_i and S_E = Σρ_h\^{n−i}·Ē_i are the drainage-weighted sums of climatological rainfall and PET over the horizon. A m_P of 1.0 means an exactly average winter suffices; m_P = 1.5 means a winter 50% wetter than average is needed.*

The critical rainfall threshold then follows directly:

$${P_{\mathit{flood}} = m_{P}}\cdot{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\overline{P_{i}}}$$

*(4) P_flood is m_P converted from a dimensionless multiplier into a depth in millimetres --- the number a site manager can compare directly against a seasonal rainfall forecast or a historical percentile. For example, a C2 well with a September minimum of 0.5 m below ground requires m_P = 1.05, giving P_flood ≈ 448 mm --- a near-average October--February total. A well requiring m_P = 2.5 has never received sufficient winter rainfall in the 95-year RAF Valley record.*

Because the weighting ρ_h\^{n−i} places greater emphasis on early-winter rainfall than on late-winter rainfall, the formulation encodes the physical fact that October recharge has more months to contribute to the peak than March recharge does, modulated by the cluster-specific drainage coefficient β₃. Three natural classes of well emerge from this framework: those whose required m_P is less than unity (P_flood reachable under sub-average winters), those requiring 1.0 ≤ m_P \< 2.5 (reachable only in wetter-than-average winters of varying rarity), and those for which m_P ≥ 2.5 (effectively unreachable under the present climate). This classification is applied spatially across the dipwell network in Section 4.

This algebraic inversion provides site managers with a dynamic, site-specific forecasting tool. By entering a measured summer minimum dipwell reading (h₀) into the cluster\'s equation, a manager obtains both the cumulative winter rainfall (mm) required to raise that well to the slack-floor threshold, and its expression as a multiple of climatological winter rainfall (m_P) --- a direct measure of ecological flooding feasibility in the subsequent recharge season.

### []{#anchor-25}Long-Term Climate Trajectory and Threshold Exceedance Analysis

To assess the long-term trajectory of slack hydrological viability, annual summer minima and winter maxima were extracted for all five clusters from the cluster-centroid time series generated during the clustering analysis. C4 and C5, both forested clusters whose water tables sit below the slack viability thresholds, are included for completeness to characterize the full network trajectory and to support future analysis of forest management effects on seasonal extremes. The hydrological year was defined as 1 October to 30 September, consistent with Section 3.6.2, and a minimum of three valid monthly observations per season was required for a year to be included.

For summer minima, ordinary least squares linear regression was fitted to the annual series for each cluster over the 2004--2026 observation window and extrapolated to 2040, with 95% confidence intervals derived analytically. Summer trajectories were plotted against the eco-hydrological viability thresholds established by Curreli et al. (2013): −0.61 m for wet slack communities (SD15b) and −0.98 m for dry slack communities (SD16).

The uncertainty in the projected year at which each cluster\'s summer-minimum trend crosses the Curreli et al. (2013) SD15b and SD16 thresholds was quantified by a year-resampling bootstrap. The annual summer-minimum series for each cluster was resampled with replacement (n = 1000 replicates); the ordinary least squares trend was refitted to each replicate; and the crossing year for each threshold was extracted from the refitted trend. The central estimate is the median of the resulting distribution of crossing years, and the 90% confidence interval is given by its 5th and 95th percentiles. Because the interval is generated from the resampled trend rather than from an analytical slope variance, it reflects both slope uncertainty and the year-to-year variability of the summer-minimum series, and is consequently wider than a parametric trend-confidence projection. The bootstrap captures sampling uncertainty in the trend slope and intercept but not model-form uncertainty --- in particular the assumption that the linear trend extrapolates cleanly into a regime where the summer minimum may approach a drainage-controlled basement --- so the resulting horizon should be read as an upper bound on viability rather than a calibrated forecast. *The procedure is implemented in 14b_year_of_crossing.py.*

For winter maxima, no reliable projection method was identified --- direct linear regression on annual winter maxima produced R² values below 0.03 across all clusters, and transfer function projection via the seasonal models of Section 3.6.2 produced physically implausible trajectories for the eastern clusters due to extrapolation beyond the fitted range. The winter analysis therefore presents the observed record only. Threshold exceedance frequency was calculated for each cluster as the proportion of hydrological years in which the winter maximum exceeded the wet slack flooding threshold of −0.10 m (SD15b) and the dry slack threshold of −0.25 m (SD16), providing a direct measure of current ecological flooding adequacy for each structural domain.

*Critical rainfall threshold equations, peak flood prediction equations, and summer drought prediction equations were implemented in 11_forecasting_thresholds.py. Climate trajectory projections and threshold exceedance analysis are implemented in 14_climate_projections.py.*

### **Spatial Distribution of Threshold Metrics**

The cluster-level threshold framework of Sections 3.6.3 and 3.6.4 is complemented by a set of per-well spatial fields that render the eco-hydrological status of every dipwell across the classified network. Four metrics are mapped. The mean summer-minimum depth is computed at each well from its annual minimum above-Ordnance-Datum water level over the August--September window, requiring at least one valid observation per year, and converted to depth below ground by subtracting the level from the LiDAR ground elevation. The mean winter-maximum depth is computed analogously from the annual maximum over the October-to-March window, requiring at least three valid observations in that window for a year to be admitted, and converted to depth below ground on the same convention. The critical rainfall threshold P_flood is evaluated at each well by applying the iterated closed-form solution of Section 3.6.3 to that well\'s observed mean summer minimum, using per-well state-space coefficients at the reference wells and cluster-centroid coefficients at the extended wells assigned through the Pearson affinity audit (Section 3.3). The winter flooding frequency is computed at each well having at least five years of winter record as the percentage of hydrological years in which the winter-maximum water table reached or exceeded the local ground surface, taking the LiDAR ground elevation as the surface datum.

Aggregating on above-Ordnance-Datum elevations renders the summer-minimum and winter-maximum metrics invariant to the ground-surface lowering produced by scraping at treatment wells; the surface change is carried instead by the depth-below-ground conversion, which applies the post-intervention ground elevation. Each per-well field is interpolated to the standard site grid by inverse-distance weighting and masked across the dune ridges where the elevation model exceeds the interpolated water surface, on the convention described in Section 3.8. The summer-minimum, winter-maximum and flooding-frequency surfaces are referenced to the eco-hydrological thresholds of Curreli et al. (2013). The spatial fields are presented in Section 4.7. *The per-well threshold metrics and their spatial fields are implemented in 11b_spatial_thresholds.py.*

## []{#anchor-26}Characterizing Water Table Losses and Long-Term Trajectories

### []{#anchor-27}**Depth-Dependent Evapotranspiration Model** 

To test whether the atmospheric draw coefficient varies significantly with water table depth --- and whether a depth-dependent formulation is warranted over the standard fixed-β₂ SSM --- an extended model was implemented in which β₂ was replaced by the depth-dependent term β₂ · exp(−κ · d_w), where d_w is the depth of the water table below ground surface (metres) and κ is a decay parameter (m⁻¹) controlling the rate at which evapotranspiration influence declines as the capillary fringe retreats from the root zone. Depth below ground surface was computed at each timestep as d_w = max(−h, 0), where h is the water table position (negative convention). No upstand term enters: h is already referenced to the ground surface (Section 3.1.1). The floor at zero keeps d_w a physical distance below ground when a slack is ponded. Because the modified predictor −exp(−κ · d_w) · PET remains linear in β₂ for any fixed κ, the three coefficients β₁, β₂ and β₃ were recovered by no-intercept OLS at each value of κ. A systematic grid search over κ ∈ \[0, 6\] m⁻¹ at intervals of 0.05 m⁻¹ was conducted independently for each cluster, with the optimal κ selected by maximizing iterative simulation NSE. Setting κ = 0 recovers the standard SSM exactly, providing a direct baseline for comparison.

Despite the statistical improvement that the grid search produces (Section 4.4), the depth-dependent formulation introduces a nonlinearity that would propagate through the threshold equations (Section 4.7), forestry scenarios (Section 4.9), and forecasting tools. The standard SSM\'s fixed β₂ provides an effective depth-averaged parameterization that preserves the closed-form analytical framework on which these operational outputs depend. The depth-dependent formulation was therefore not adopted for the primary analysis; the standard fixed-β₂ SSM is retained throughout. The fixed β₂ should be understood as absorbing a real depth-coupling effect whose magnitude varies across clusters; its diagnostic significance is discussed further in Section 5.6.1. *The depth-dependent PET grid search and benchmark comparison are implemented in 15_depth_dependent_pet.py.*

### []{#anchor-28}**Mean Monthly Water Balance Decomposition**

Water balance decomposition of the kind applied here --- partitioning monthly head change into recharge, evaporative draw, drainage and residual --- has a long history in the coastal dune hydrology literature, particularly in the Dutch and North Sea coastal systems where managed water tables and dune slack conservation drive analogous restoration questions (Stuyfzand, 1993; Grootjans et al., 2002, 2017). The decomposition applied in this study derives the component fluxes directly from the fitted SSM coefficients, allowing direct comparison of fluxes across clusters subject to identical climate forcing using only the dipwell and climate records already available for the site.

To quantify and compare the hydrological inputs and losses operating on each hydrogeological cluster, a mean monthly water balance decomposition was applied to the five principal clusters (C1--C5) using cluster-level SSM coefficients derived in Section 3.4.1. All terms are expressed in metres of water table change per month (m/month), the natural unit of the state-space model and directly comparable across clusters receiving the same climate forcing.

The decomposition isolates three components from the canonical state-space equation (Section 3.4):

$$\Delta{h = \beta_{1}}\cdot P-\beta_{2}\cdot\mathit{PET}-\beta_{3}\cdot h_{\mathit{disp}}$$

Mean monthly recharge was computed as β₁ × P̄ , where P̄ is the mean monthly precipitation over the monitoring period from the RAF Valley record. Atmospheric draw was computed as β₂ × PET̄ , where PET̄ is the mean monthly Thornthwaite PET. Gravity drainage was computed as β₃ × h̄ \_disp, where h̄ \_disp is the mean displacement above the drainage datum (h̄ \_disp = z₀ + h̄ , with z₀ = 3.7 m; see Section 3.4) for each cluster derived from the cluster-average hydrograph. Because the drainage term scales with displacement above the datum, the drainage/ET partition depends on the datum regime: a datum set within the water-table fluctuation range reduces the drainage term to mean-reversion of anomalies and attributes almost no steady flux to drainage, whereas at depths beyond the fluctuation range the term represents Darcy outflow above a fixed base and the partition is insensitive to the exact choice. The 3.7 m datum sits within this stable Darcy regime (Section 3.4; the supporting datum-regime diagnostic is presented in Supplementary Material Note S9). For the Main Forest cluster (C4), where this datum sensitivity is greatest, an identifiability diagnostic confirms that the low drainage coefficient is cleanly recovered at the cluster-centroid scale --- C4 has among the lowest predictor collinearity in the network (VIF ≈ 1.1, second-lowest of the five clusters) --- so the drainage/ET partition is well determined there rather than a fitting artefact (Section 5.2.3). Canopy interception is not included as a separate loss term --- it is implicitly captured in the forested clusters\' (C4 and C5) lower β₁ and lower β₂, and adding it explicitly would double-count losses already embedded in the fitted coefficients. Total losses are therefore the sum of atmospheric draw and drainage only. The net monthly balance --- recharge minus total losses --- quantifies the water balance residual --- the flux that would be required from some unmodelled source to maintain long-run water table equilibrium.

A companion volumetric partition is presented alongside the primary head-space decomposition (Table 4b; Figure 11a), expressing the recharge, evapotranspiration and drainage terms as annual depths (mm yr⁻¹). The partition is obtained from the head-space fractions applied to the net climate input (precipitation less canopy interception), without a specific-yield conversion; the split between evapotranspiration and drainage is bracketed by two independent estimates --- the SSM head-space ratios and the observed seasonal recession rates --- and the range between them is shown as a hatched band at the evapotranspiration/drainage boundary in Figure 11b. For the forested clusters (C4 and C5), canopy interception is shown as an explicit segment on the inputs bar of Figure 11a, computed as 0.24 × P̄ following Freeman (2008), reducing the net input rather than being additive. The mean monthly water balance decomposition and volumetric partition were produced by 16_water_bal.py (outputs: 16_water_bal_table.csv, 16_water_bal_vol_table.csv).

### []{#anchor-29}**Specific Yield Estimation: Water Table Fluctuation Method**

To characterise the substrate storage capacity independently of the head-space water balance --- and to compare against the literature specific-yield range for unconfined dune sand (C1 = 0.08 over glacial till, C2--C5 = 0.12; Fetter, 2001) --- an independent estimation of the specific yield (Sy) was performed using the water table fluctuation (WTF) method of Healy and Cook (2002):

$${S_{y} = \frac{R}{\Delta}}h$$

where R is the net recharge reaching the water table (m) and Δh is the corresponding water table rise (m).

Three complementary derivations of Sy are reported. Approach A (through-origin OLS) fits a linear regression of corrected water-table rise against net recharge for each cluster over the winter months (November--March, PET \< 25 mm/month), with the regression forced through the origin so that the slope is the cluster-mean Sy. The water-table rise is corrected for storage decay by adding the drainage component β₃·\|h_prev\| derived from the SSM, isolating the recharge-driven rise from the contemporaneous drainage loss. Approach B (event median) computes a per-month Sy = R / Δh for each rising-limb event in the record (months where Δh \> 5 mm and net recharge P − PET \> 10 mm), with event-level estimates further constrained to the physically plausible range 0.01 \< Sy \< 0.50 to exclude months where the suppressed or negative Δh signal produced implausibly high individual Sy values; the cluster-mean Sy is reported as the median of the event distribution with interquartile range as the uncertainty bound. Approach C (rapid recharge events, after Crosbie et al., 2005) is a third, methodologically independent estimator: rather than correcting for drainage (as Approach A does through β₃) or ignoring it (as Approach B does), it selects short, sharply-rising episodes in which drainage during the rise is negligible by construction. A candidate episode requires at least two consecutive prior months of falling or static water table (Δh ≤ 0), begins on the first rising month, extends for at most two further months while the rise continues, and must accumulate a cumulative rise of at least 50 mm; the per-episode Sy is the accumulated net recharge over the episode divided by the cumulative rise, filtered to the same 0.01--0.50 plausibility range as Approach B, with the cluster estimate taken as the median of qualifying episodes and a 1000-sample bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Forest clusters carry the same Freeman (2008) interception correction as Approach B. Approach B is the canonical figure used by downstream water-balance scripts; Approaches A and C are reported alongside as independent methods cross-checks and neither propagates to any downstream calculation. Agreement among the three approaches on the cluster ordering is taken as evidence that the specific-yield gradient is robust to the choice of estimation strategy, while divergences at individual clusters are interpreted as diagnostic of the estimators\' differing sensitivities rather than as a ranking between them.

All three approaches are applied to the cluster-mean hydrographs derived in Section 3.4.1. Monthly data cannot isolate individual storm events, and the WTF method at monthly resolution is known to overestimate effective Sy because it cannot separate true gravity drainage from capillary fringe release (Healy and Cook, 2002; Scanlon et al., 2002). The resulting estimates should therefore be interpreted as upper bounds on Sy rather than point estimates of the long-term effective value.

For the Forest clusters (C4 and C5), a correction was applied for canopy interception prior to computing net recharge:

$${R_{\mathit{eff}} = \left( {1-0.24} \right)}\cdot P-\mathit{PET}$$

following the site-specific interception fraction of Freeman (2008). Only the precipitation term is reduced. The PET term is retained unchanged because Thornthwaite PET is an energy-based atmospheric demand derived from temperature and day length, independent of land cover; it represents the capacity of the atmosphere to receive water vapour rather than the realized evaporative flux from any particular surface. Reducing PET to account for canopy-evaporated intercepted water would conflate atmospheric demand with actual evapotranspiration and remove the same quantity from both sides of the water balance. Without the interception correction, months in which canopy suppression of Δh is most pronounced produce individual Sy estimates above the plausibility threshold and are excluded from the event pool; applying the correction recovers these months, increases the event count, and lowers the event-median Sy at both forest clusters by repopulating the event pool with below-median values (see Section 4.2.4 and Table 4c). Approach A interception-corrected variants were tested but found to be unstable in this dataset, and are not reported; the Approach B forest values cited in Section 4.2.4 use the corrected event pool.

Results of the cluster-level and well-level WTF analyses are presented in Section 4.2.4. *The cluster-level analysis was implemented in 17_wtf_specific_yield.py and the well-level spatial analysis in 18_wtf_spatial.py.*

### Network-Scale Coastal-Retreat Gradient Regression

To partition each cluster\'s observed summer-minimum decline into a climate-driven component and a coastal-retreat-driven component, a non-linear panel regression was fitted to the full 21-year monthly record. Each well\'s perpendicular distance to the eroding Caernarfon Bay High Water Mark was computed within the pipeline from a committed OpenStreetMap mean-high-water coastline (EPSG:27700) restricted to the 15 km west-facing Newborough shoreline; the Menai Strait and Llanddwyn Island were excluded as non-eroding boundaries.

Two functional forms were fitted: a Dupuit--Forchheimer steady-state strip-aquifer form,

$$\delta{(d) = \mathit{\max}}{\left( {\delta_{0}\cdot\left( {1-{d/L_{\mathit{cg}}}} \right),0} \right) + c_{\mathit{far}}}$$

and an exponential decay form,

$$\delta{(d) = \delta_{0}}\cdot\exp{\left( {{-d}/L_{\mathit{cg}}} \right) + c_{\mathit{far}}}$$

where d is distance from the coast, δ_0 is the coast-edge water-table deepening rate above climate, L_cg is the inland reach, and c_far is the far-field climate background. Both were fitted by profile non-linear least squares, with well and month fixed effects and a cumulative-water-balance covariate absorbed by within-well demeaning. Model selection between the two functional forms used the Akaike Information Criterion. Three nested specifications were fitted to test robustness to forest-cover inclusion: the full network (72 wells, all clusters minus the BACI clearfell-zone wells), a forest-free specification dropping all C4 and C5 wells, and a C3-only specification using the 17 non-forested C3 wells alone. The forest-free linear-with-cutoff fit is taken as the headline. A fourth fit controls forest cover explicitly rather than by exclusion --- the full network with a canopy × time term on the wells' land-cover flag --- and returns an essentially unchanged coast-edge amplitude alongside a separate −9.0 ± 2.5 mm yr⁻¹ deepening absorbed under pine, so the gradient does not depend on how forest cover is handled.

The headline fit is then applied to the per-cluster decomposition of the long-term summer-minimum slope into gradient and climate components (Section 4.10.2). *The network-scale coastal-retreat gradient regression is implemented in 25_coastal_gradient.py.*

### **Five-Year Mean Spring Water Level (MSL5) and Associated Forecasting Tools**

The seasonal prediction equations of Section 3.6.2 and the critical rainfall threshold of Section 3.6.3 operate in summer-minimum and winter-peak space, against the eco-hydrological thresholds of Curreli et al. (2013). Van Willegen et al. (2025) revisited the eco-hydrological calibration for the Newborough dune slacks using a larger vegetation dataset and a wider set of candidate hydrological metrics, and identified the unweighted five-year mean spring water level as the best-performing predictor of community-mean vegetation moisture response. This metric, here denoted MSL5, is computed across the monitoring network as a complement to the summer-minimum framework. Three analytical components are described in turn: the MSL5 metric itself, an empirical transfer function that forecasts the next spring\'s mean level, and a climate-scenario projection of the metric.

**The MSL5 metric.** For each well, the annual mean spring water level for hydrological year *y* is the unweighted mean of the March, April and May values of that year. To place the entire antecedent forcing window within a single hydrological year, the van Willegen hydrological year is defined as 1 June (*y*−1) to 31 May (*y*) --- distinct from the October-commencing hydrological year used for the seasonal equations of Section 3.6.2, and adopted here so that the spring response window and its winter and spring antecedents share one annual unit. The five-year mean spring water level MSL5, indexed by its closing year, is the unweighted mean of five consecutive annual spring means.
