Two completeness rules are applied: all three spring months must be present in the quality-controlled record for an annual spring mean to be admitted --- presence includes the isolated single-month gap-fills of Section 3.1.1, which are admitted and tracked per window rather than excluded --- and all five constituent annual means must be valid for a five-year mean to be admitted; windows containing any excluded annual mean are themselves excluded rather than bridged. Across the study record the gap-fill provision is marginal: 13 of 1302 admitted annual spring means (1.0%) and 28 of 895 admitted five-year windows (3.1%) contain an interpolated month, never more than one; the per-window counts are carried in the committed Script 26 outputs. The metric is computed at every well with sufficient record and aggregated to cluster level as the unweighted mean of member-well values. Levels are reported below ground surface, the convention of the source study, which the ground-referenced records of Section 3.1.1 already provide without further correction.

**The spring MSL transfer function.** To allow the coming spring\'s mean level to be forecast before the season closes, an empirical transfer function was fitted independently for each of the five clusters, predicting the annual spring mean from antecedent winter and spring conditions:

$${\mathit{MSL}_{y} = \alpha_{W}}\cdot{h_{\mathit{\max},\mathit{winter}} + b}\cdot{P_{\mathit{win}-\mathit{spr}} + \gamma}\cdot{\mathit{PET}_{\mathit{win}-\mathit{spr}} + c}$$

where $$\mathit{MSL}_{y}$$ is the cluster-centroid mean of the March--May water levels in hydrological year *y*; $$h_{\mathit{\max},\mathit{winter}}$$ is the cluster-centroid maximum head over October (*y*−1) to February (*y*); $$P_{\mathit{win}-\mathit{spr}}$$and $$\mathit{PET}_{\mathit{win}-\mathit{spr}}$$ are cumulative precipitation and Thornthwaite PET over October (*y*−1) to May (*y*); and $$c$$ is a fitted intercept. The coefficients are fitted by ordinary least squares with an intercept term, using the cluster-centroid monthly series --- the same baseline against which the cluster state-space coefficients of Section 3.4.1 are fitted, ensuring internal consistency between the empirical transfer function and the mechanistic model. The winter peak enters as the antecedent-state term and carries the aquifer memory between seasons, in the same role as the antecedent terms in the Section 3.6.2 seasonal equations. The transfer function gives managers a forecast of the coming spring mean from readings already in hand by late winter, which can be combined with the rolling record of recent observed annual means to update the MSL5 statistic ahead of the end-of-spring readings.

**Climate-scenario projection.** To place the MSL5 metric in the context of projected climate change, a perturbation overlay was computed under UKCP18 RCP8.5 central-estimate scenarios for the 2050s and 2080s. For each cluster and scenario, a monthly water-table perturbation is computed from the cluster\'s state-space coefficients and the scenario climate departure:

$$\Delta h{(m) = \beta_{1}}\cdot\left( {P_{\mathit{scen}}(m)-P_{\mathit{base}}(m)} \right)-\beta_{2}\cdot\left( {\mathit{PET}_{\mathit{scen}}(m)-\mathit{PET}_{\mathit{base}}(m)} \right)$$

where $$\beta_{1}$$ and $$\beta_{2}$$ are the cluster recharge and atmospheric-draw coefficients of Section 3.4.1; $$P_{\mathit{base}}(m)$$ and $$\mathit{PET}_{\mathit{base}}(m)$$ are the long-term monthly climatology over the monitoring period; and $$P_{\mathit{scen}}(m)$$ and $$\mathit{PET}_{\mathit{scen}}(m)$$ apply seasonal UKCP18 multipliers to that climatology. This is the seasonal-perturbation formulation also used in the forestry scenario analysis (Section 3.5.4 and the scenario evaluation of the pipeline), expressing a scenario as a departure from baseline climate rather than as an equilibrium displacement. Because the perturbation is linear in precipitation and PET and the scenario multipliers are a stationary shift in climatology rather than an interannual sequence, the projected change in MSL5 is a single constant per cluster and scenario --- the mean of the perturbations over the three spring months --- and the projected MSL5 trajectory is the observed trajectory shifted vertically by that constant. The projection is therefore a climatological response under stationary observed variability: it characterizes the sensitivity of MSL5 to a shift in mean climate, and is not a forward-in-time forecast of the level that will be observed in any particular future year.

*The MSL5 metric and its forecasting and projection companions sit alongside, and do not replace, the summer-minimum framework of Sections 3.6 and 4.8; the two measure the same multi-year hydrological state through different seasonal windows. The MSL5 aggregation is implemented in 26_van_willegen_msl.py; the spring transfer function in Section 5 of 11_forecasting_thresholds.py; and the UKCP18 projection in 26b_van_willegen_msl_projections.py.*

###  Equilibrium Wetness Index and Vegetation Cross-Validation

The MSL5 metric of Section 3.7.5 measures spring wetness directly from the water-level record; the state-space model of Section 3.4.1 offers a structural counterpart computed from the fitted coefficients. Section 3.7.5 sets aside the equilibrium-displacement form of the model in favour of a seasonal perturbation for climate projection; here that same equilibrium form is used not for projection but to define a static wetness index, calibrated against MSL5 and cross-validated against independent vegetation data.

**The equilibrium wetness index. **Setting the mean monthly change to zero in the state-space model (Section 3.4.1) and solving the head-dependent drainage term for the steady-state displacement gives h_disp,eq = (β₁·P̄ − β₂·PET̄)/β₃, whence the equilibrium wetness index EWI = h_disp,eq − z₀, reported below ground surface to match the MSL5 convention, the records being ground-referenced (Section 3.1.1). Here β₁, β₂, β₃ are the per-well recharge, atmospheric-draw and drainage coefficients; z₀ is the drainage datum (3.7 m); and P̄, PET̄ are the full-record monthly-mean precipitation and Thornthwaite PET --- the same long-term climatology used as the projection baseline in Section 3.7.5. Because the forcing is the long-term normal rather than a specific observation window, the index is climate-window-independent, estimating a well\'s intrinsic wetness from its response coefficients alone and computable from a shorter record than MSL5 requires. Two network tiers are distinguished: reference wells take the quality-controlled coefficients of Section 3.4.1, while extended wells are fitted with the same shared state-space routine as a single pass without that control, and flagged accordingly. Wells whose drainage coefficient is near zero or negative (CEH13, CEH14) are excluded, that coefficient being the denominator of the equilibrium expression.

**Uncertainty in the index.** The equilibrium expression is a ratio, so uncertainty in the fitted coefficients propagates into the index. Because the drainage datum z₀ is a constant, subtracting it shifts the equilibrium displacement without changing its uncertainty; the propagation is therefore anchored on h_disp,eq itself rather than on the datum-referenced index value, which would understate the error at wells whose equilibrium level lies close to the datum. Two variants are computed. The first propagates the drainage coefficient alone: since h_disp,eq is inversely proportional to β₃, the relative error in β₃ passes directly into the index, and this dominant term is the variant quoted below. The second is a first-order propagation over all three coefficients treated as independent --- a close approximation rather than an exact joint interval, given the mild collinearity between the recharge and atmospheric-draw terms. Standard errors for reference wells are recovered from the committed coefficient, its two-sided p-value and the sample size, the t statistic inverting exactly for the no-intercept three-predictor model; extended-tier fits return standard errors directly from the shared fitting routine.

**Calibration onto the spring-level scale. **The index sits on a systematically deeper scale than the observed spring level and is calibrated onto the MSL5 scale by ordinary least squares, MSL5 = a + b·EWI, across the wells carrying both. Consistent with MSL5\'s open-dune character (Section 4.8.2) and with the forest coefficients being the least constrained on the site (Sections 3.4.4, 4.9.2), the calibration is scoped to the open-dune network (clusters C1--C3); forest wells (C4, C5) are predicted but reported out of scope. Cluster membership for reference wells follows Section 3.4.1, and for extended wells the Pearson affinity analysis of Section 3.3.

**Vegetation cross-validation. **To test both metrics against the ecological target directly, the co-located Ellenberg-F moisture indicator values (the wetness indicator, scale 1--12; Hill et al., 1999) of van Willegen et al. (2025) were obtained from the associated open dataset (van Willegen et al., 2024) and aggregated to a mean per piezometer. Observed MSL5 and the equilibrium index were each regressed on mean Ellenberg-F between wells, and the difference between the two correlations --- dependent, since they share the response variable --- was tested by Williams\' test (Williams, 1959). This cross-validation draws on an external dataset and is computed once rather than as part of the recurring pipeline.

The equilibrium wetness index and its MSL5 comparison are implemented in 26_van_willegen_msl.py; the vegetation cross-validation uses the van Willegen open dataset.

## []{#anchor-30}Spatial Analysis

### Baseline Fields, Combined Drivers and Network Change

This subsection presents the spatial fields that characterize the aquifer's baseline state and its change over the monitoring period, in three groups: two baseline products derived directly from the per-well SSM parameterization; a group of maps that combine or difference the active drivers; and a group that characterizes observed network change directly, independently of the driver model. All are rendered on the standard 50 m British National Grid (EPSG:27700) site grid and site-polygon clip described in Section 3.8.2. The two baseline products are (1) the mean annual water-table surface, from which the groundwater flow-direction field is derived; and (2) the state-space water-balance residual field, which maps how completely the three-term model closes the long-term balance at each well. The mean annual water-table surface is constructed by inverse-distance-weighted interpolation of each well\'s mean above-Ordnance-Datum head over the monitoring period to the 50 m grid, masked to the sea-boundary extent. No elevation-model mask is applied to this surface, because the water table is a continuous field independent of the overlying dune topography. From the interpolated head surface, groundwater flow-direction vectors are obtained as the negative head gradient,

$${Q = -}K\cdot b\cdot\nabla h$$

(Bear, 1972; Freeze and Cherry, 1979), evaluated by finite differences across the grid, then normalized to unit length and reported as direction only. The hydraulic conductivity K = 6.0 m day⁻¹ (Betson et al., 2002) and the interpolated aquifer-thickness surface b therefore set the orientation of the field rather than a calibrated flux magnitude, and vectors falling on ridge interpolation artefacts are suppressed. The vectors are reported as directional context for the interpolated head field, not as the output of a calibrated continuous-flow model.

The state-space water-balance residual field expresses, at each reference well, the degree to which the three-term model closes the long-term balance. Setting the monthly change to zero at long-run equilibrium, the residual is the excess of modelled losses over modelled recharge,

$${\alpha_{B} = \left( {\beta_{2}\cdot{\overline{\mathit{PET}} + \beta_{3}}\cdot\overline{h_{\mathit{disp}}}} \right)}-\beta_{1}\cdot\overline{P}$$

where the overbars denote long-term monthly means, overline h_disp is the mean displacement above the drainage datum (Section 3.4), overline PET is Thornthwaite potential evaporation --- above-canopy at the forested clusters and open-dune elsewhere --- and overline P is gross rainfall; both are taken uncorrected at every cluster, including the forested ones (Section 3.8). A positive residual marks a location where the rainfall-driven recharge captured by the model does not account for the observed head --- an inadequacy in the three-term model at that location, or in principle an unmodelled input; a negative residual marks slight over-prediction. On the present evidence the diagnostic reading is the supported one (Sections 4.9.6, 5.2.1). The residual is computed from the fitted β coefficients alone --- specific yield does not enter --- and interpolated to the site grid with zero-valued anchors along the sea and estuary boundaries and the dune ridges masked. The head surface, flow field and residual field are presented in Section 4.9.

The remaining figures extend the analysis beyond the baseline state. The first group combines or differences the active drivers: a measured clearfell step-change map, a parametric net state map combining all five active drivers, a 2005→2025 driver-change map, and an empirical MSL5 change map. The second group characterizes observed network change directly, independently of the driver model.

The clearfell step-change map (Figure 60) is derived from the climate-corrected difference in mean water-table level between the pre-felling scraping era and the post-felling era at each well (fell_step_cc, Script 10b; Section 3.5.4), converted to millimetres. Values are interpolated to the site grid using IDW (power 1.5) with a 100 m Gaussian blur applied within the site polygon to suppress single-well artefacts. Well markers use the same discrete banded diverging colourmap as the surface (±150 mm symmetric scale, 14 bands) to ensure self-consistency between data points and the interpolated field. Seventy wells pass the quality filter (minimum six post-felling monthly observations required to estimate a stable post-felling era mean; wells with data-quality flags excluded). This map shares its underlying per-well values with the climate-corrected clearfell map of the BACI analysis (Figure 34; Section 4.6.5); the two renders differ in convention rather than data --- Figure 34 uses a continuous, data-scaled colour range on a finer 40 m interpolation grid with cluster-coded markers, serving the BACI evidence, whereas the fixed banded scale and Gaussian smoothing here place the felling step on the common footing of the driver-map group. Implemented in *20_spatial_figures.py*.

**The parametric net state map **(Figure 61) superimposes five annual-mean driver fields on the site grid. Each field uses an exponential decay H₀ × exp(−d/λ) from the relevant source geometry, where λ = √(Kb/Syβ₃) ≈ 230 m (K = 6.0 m day⁻¹, b = 5 m, Sy = 0.306, β₃ = 0.0569 month⁻¹ from the C3 cluster centroid). The reach is a scaling estimate rather than a calibrated length: hydraulic conductivity is a literature value for dune sand, and across the range reported for that material (2--20 m day⁻¹) λ spans roughly 130--420 m, while the assumed 5 m aquifer thickness (3--8 m) spans 180--290 m. The drainage datum contributes less than either, β₃ varying by about a quarter over a plausible datum range and λ with its square root. The results below are therefore stated to the nearest tens of metres, and the conclusions they support depend only on the reach being of order 200 m rather than of order 20 m or 2 km. The five components are: (i) forest canopy drawdown --- loss, H₀ = 150 mm, decaying from the forest boundary, zeroed over the felling polygon; (ii) clearfell gain --- positive, same H₀ and λ, decaying from the felling polygon boundary; (iii) scrape drain --- loss, H₀ = 129 mm anchored to the measured CEH36 response, same λ; (iv) coastal erosion drawdown --- loss, h₀ = 81 mm at the dune toe from the 6 m Storm Brendan exemplar retreat and the live Script 25 fit; (v) sea-level-rise head gain --- positive, +20 mm over five years at the shore. Net = SLR + clearfell − forest − erosion − scrape. A first-order superposition of single-mechanism illustrative annual-mean fields; not a closed water balance. Implemented in *20_spatial_figures.py*.

**The 2005→2025 driver-change map **(Figure 62) re-bases the net-state construction to the monitoring record, differencing each modelled driver field between its 2005 and 2025 states so that the map shows what the drivers imply should have changed over the study window rather than the accumulated state since the forest was planted. Because the standing pine canopy is at equilibrium at both endpoints, its drawdown cancels in the difference and the mature forest interior returns to near zero, confirming the map is an epoch difference rather than a re-drawing of Figure 61. Five fields change over the window and are summed: the clearfell gain, as in the net-state map; the dune-scrape response, with all cuts within the window contributing; a broadleaf-restock field new to this map, computed on the same exponential-decay construction but scaled by the broadleaf interception fraction (0.15, against 0.24 for pine; Komatsu et al., 2011) and by the 2005→2025 canopy-establishment increment, giving of order 56 mm of added drawdown at source and appearing as a loss patch of the opposite sign to the clearfell gain; the five-year chronic coastal drawdown, five years of the observed coast-edge decline rate δ₀ fitted in Section 4.10.2, applied at the dune toe on the same five-year horizon as the sea-level-rise field; and the sea-level-rise head gain over the same span. As a first-order superposition the map is illustrative and not a closed water balance; the broadleaf and coastal fields in particular are modelled quantities the dipwell record cannot fully resolve, and are presented as indicative. It is the modelled companion to the absolute climate-removed trend map (Figure 65) over the same window. *Implemented in 20_spatial_figures.py.*

**The empirical MSL5 change map **(Figure 63) is the observed counterpart of the modelled driver maps. For each well with a valid five-year mean spring water level (Section 3.7.5) at both window ends, it differences the current MSL5 window ending 2023 (springs 2019--2023) against the last complete pre-clearfell window ending 2017 (springs 2013--2017), taking the raw below-ground difference with no common-mode normalization: the five-year spring mean already averages inter-annual climate noise, and differential wet-year memory at slow-draining wells is not removable by a common-mode subtraction. The 2023 current window is the canonical choice, validated by the three independent checks of Section 5.7.5; the 2012 drought year falls outside both windows. Values are drawn from the Script 26 per-well MSL5 series with the MSL5 well exclusions honoured, and interpolated to the site grid by IDW (power 2) with a one-cell Gaussian blur applied within the site polygon; changes below ±25 mm --- the MSL5 measurement noise floor after five-year averaging --- are left uncoloured. Implemented in *20_spatial_figures.py*.

The four following network-change maps are constructed from the same per-well spring (March--May) series and differ only in climate handling and frame of reference; Supplementary Material Note S10 gives a comparison table and construction schematic. Two of the maps remove the common climate signal by subtracting the network-mean spring: the differential-movement map (Figure 64) asks which wells are gaining or losing ground against the site as a whole (mm yr⁻¹, relative to the site mean), and the amplification field (Figure 66) asks how strongly each well swings between dry and wet springs (a ratio to the network-mean swing). Two maps work in each well's absolute frame: the absolute climate-removed trend map (Figure 65) asks how fast each well itself is drifting once the shared climate signal is removed (mm yr⁻¹, per well), and the dry-year spring depth map (Figure 67) asks how close a dry spring already sits to the ecological thresholds (metres below ground). Neither of the two accompanying analyses adds a further map: the per-well climate-sensitivity coefficient (Script 35) is a discrete companion to the amplification field (Figure 66), extending that metric to short-record wells, and the two-window sensitivity demonstration (Script 34) is presented in Supplementary Material Note S11.

****The differential-movement map ****(Figure 64) isolates the secular component of spring water-table change that the two-window MSL5 comparison cannot resolve. For each well a spring value is formed for every year as the mean of the available March--May readings; the well\'s anomaly is its spring level minus the site-mean spring level in the same year, the subtraction removing the common climate signal so that what remains is movement relative to the network as a whole. The site-mean reference panel is restricted to the wells present in a fixed majority fraction of the period\'s springs, so the reference does not drift with coverage. The per-well metric is the ordinary-least-squares slope of this anomaly against year, in millimetres per year, fitted over two periods --- 2011--2025 (primary) and 2005--2025 (robustness). Significance is assessed by a lag-1 autoregression-corrected t-test on the effective sample size and cross-checked against a moving-block bootstrap confidence interval; significant wells are drawn solid and non-significant wells hollow. Only the Llyn Rhos-Ddu lake gauge is excluded --- CEH13 and CEH14, withheld from the SSM analyses for state-space reasons, are retained here because the differential anomaly trend is purely observational and does not use the model. The per-well slopes are interpolated to the 50 m grid by inverse-distance weighting (power 2), masked beyond 450 m of the nearest well. Because the anomaly is referenced to the network mean, this map shows relative movement --- which well gains or loses ground against the site as a whole --- rather than the absolute rate of change at each well, which is mapped separately (Figure 65). *Implemented in 32_differential_movement.py.*

**The absolute climate-removed trend map **(Figure 65) complements the differential map by giving each well\'s secular rate of change on its own terms, with the shared climate signal removed but without re-referencing to the network mean. Where the differential map subtracts the site-mean spring level --- which over a wet-spring-lifted window can invert the reading, so that a well holding its position against a rising mean appears to fall --- the absolute map removes only the variance attributable to an external climate index, leaving the real site-wide recharge decline and coastal drying in the result. Spring values are formed as for the differential map. The external index is the spring climatic water balance, the sum of precipitation minus Thornthwaite PET over March--May, taken from the RAF Valley record contemporaneously with the spring level and without lag. For each well a single joint regression is fitted, h(t) = a + b·CWB(t) + c·t, and the secular trend is the fitted time coefficient c in millimetres per year; fitting the climate index and the linear trend together orthogonalizes the two, so the climate term cannot absorb the secular signal. A two-step alternative --- regressing level on the climate index and then fitting a trend to the residual --- was rejected because over a climatically non-stationary window the climate index itself trends and absorbs the real drying before the slope is measured. A coverage filter admits a well to a window only where it carries at least one spring observation before 2011 and its observed record spans at least 80% of the window, excluding short-record wells whose trend would otherwise be fitted to a truncated drought-recovery trajectory. Two periods are fitted --- 2005--2025 (primary) and 2011--2025 (robustness); the longer window is primary here, in contrast to the differential map, because the shorter window is dominated by post-2011 short-record wells. Significance, exclusions and marker convention follow the differential map. The per-well slopes are interpolated to the 50 m grid by linear interpolation within the convex hull of the wells, extended 100 m beyond the hull to reach the coastal margin, and clipped to the site polygon. Over 2005--2025 the coastal-forest cluster carries the most negative climate-removed trend (C5 ≈ −11.6 mm yr⁻¹), consistent with the coastal-retreat gradient of Section 3.7.4; the strongest individual driers are the coastal and western wells. I*mplemented in 36_absolute_climate_trend.py.*

**The climate-response envelope** (Figure 66) characterizes the range the spring water table moves between its dry and wet extremes and yields two window-independent products. Spring values are formed as for the differential map. Dry and wet extreme states are taken as the per-well mean spring level over fixed sets of extreme years, selected by site-mean spring extremity and antecedent-rainfall consistency --- dry {2011, 2012, 2019} and wet {2014, 2021, 2024}; the year 2006 is excluded as a wet extreme because its 2004--2005 antecedent was the driest in the record and the slow-draining forest wells had not refilled by that spring. Each well\'s swing is its wet state minus its dry state, and its amplification coefficient is that swing divided by the network-mean swing, with the common-mode swing removed, so that values above one magnify the shared climate forcing and below one damp it. The drought-floor surface (Figure 67) is the dry-state depth to water, retained in absolute depth below ground and contoured against the Curreli et al. (2013) SD15b (0.61 m) and SD16 (0.98 m) thresholds, which are absolute distances to surface rather than relative quantities. As in the differential map, only the lake gauge is excluded; CEH13 and CEH14 are included because the coefficient is observational. The amplification field is interpolated to the 50 m grid by linear interpolation, masked beyond 450 m of the nearest well; the drought-floor surface is likewise linearly interpolated with a ridge mask applied to suppress extrapolation onto the bedrock ridge, and the single raised inter-slack well CEH10 is shown as a distinct slack-edge marker but excluded from the interpolated slack-floor surface, which would otherwise smear its raised-ground depth across the neighbouring slacks.* Implemented in 33_envelope_amplification.py.*

The short-coverage wells that the amplification field (Figure 66) cannot interpolate are not dropped but shown on it as filled triangles, each carrying the same co-temporal climate-sensitivity coefficient (utils/envelope_metric.py) used for the surface: the well\'s dry-to-wet spring swing normalized against a reference core of full-coverage wells, with the core swing recomputed over that well\'s own extreme years, so that wells measured on different subsets of extreme springs remain comparable. Each coefficient carries a confidence tier (A: at least two dry and two wet years --- the wells that build the surface; B: at least one of each; C: a single year on one side) and a delete-one-extreme-year jackknife 90% interval. Script 35 develops this coefficient as a standalone per-well product for Paper 1 and cross-calibrates it against the independently fitted SSM response --- it correlates with the per-well β₂ and β₃ coefficients, and is reported as consistent with, rather than confirming, that response, since at the short-record wells that are its main use case the β coefficients are not available for direct cross-check. Computed across the whole network the coefficient reproduces the earlier matched-window amplification (r ≈ 0.99), confirming the field is not an artefact of the window choice. *Implemented in 35_per_well_amplification.py.*

**The two-window sensitivity demonstration** (Script 34) tests directly whether the two-window MSL5 change measures secular decline or merely the choice of windows. Per-well MSL5 for a window ending in year Y is the mean spring level over years Y−4 to Y (from the committed van Willegen aggregation, 26_msl_annual_per_well.csv), and a well qualifies for a window only if all five spring-years are present. For each ordered pair of windows the site-mean change is the mean, over the common panel of wells qualifying in both windows, of the per-well change, with the panel held fixed across the pair so composition change cannot inflate the result; admissible pairs are those whose common panel reaches at least forty wells, which excludes only the thin seven-well 2005--2009 baseline. Placing the single 2017→2023 comparison inside the envelope of every admissible pair shows the site-mean change reverses sign and spans −136 to +221 mm, so the −97 mm headline is one interior cell of a wide distribution and the two-window method characterises window choice as much as secular change. The full envelope and its figure are given in Supplementary Material Note S11 (Figure S11.1).

****Driver validation (Script 37).**** The 2005→2025 driver-change map described above presents what the modelled fields imply should have changed; Script 37 tests that implication against the observed change directly. Per-well climate-corrected endpoint differences (the absolute climate-removed trend of Figure 65) are regressed on the same unit driver fields at their modelled amplitudes, per window, with a free spatially-uniform intercept, using ordinary least squares with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Three windows are fitted: a pre-intervention window (2006--2012, coastal field only), a post-clearfell window (2018--2025, coastal and clearfell fields), and the full record (2005--2025). The intercept absorbs the site-wide recharge decline, so a uniform background drying cannot be attributed to the coastal gradient; the resulting scale factors are dimensionless multipliers on the modelled amplitude, unity meaning the aquifer feels exactly the modelled field. C2 Dune, carrying no driver field, serves as a driver-free negative control, and the sluice-controlled C1 Lake Edge wells are excluded from the fit as management-influenced. This is a validation, not a fitting step: it sets no amplitude used elsewhere. Its outcome is a bounded null --- every fitted scale factor has a confidence interval spanning both zero and unity, so the network can neither confirm the modelled amplitude nor exclude it. The modelled coastal field in particular cannot be independently recovered from the monitoring record (Section 5.7); the coastal shape it tests is moreover fitted from the same network (Section 3.7.4), making the validation partly self-confirming, with only an expanding-window trajectory of the implied coastal rate serving as an independent check (Figure 68). *Implemented in 37_driver_validation.py.*

****Comparative driver footing (Script 37b).**** The same modelled fields are placed on a common footing over the 2005→2025 window, with each driver entered as its gain and loss components (forest as clearfell and broadleaf restock, scraping as on-site rise and off-site drain cone, coast as sea-level rise and erosion drawdown). In this report the drivers are compared on three common currencies --- peak local head change (mm), area-integrated volume, and ecological-threshold crossings --- shown as grouped bars in Figure 69, with amplitudes taken from the observed BACI anchors and the modelled Script 20 fields, not the Script 37 scale factors; the peak-and-reach view of the same drivers, as depth-against-distance profiles, is the reach panel of Figure 73. The area-integrated volumetric construction that underlies the net scraping-versus-coast ratio reported in Section 4.12 is set out in Supplement §S.20.6, where the full three-currency construction and its specific-yield conversion are given; fields are superposed linearly, a first-order construction that is an upper bound in overlap zones. *Implemented in 37b_driver_footing.py.*

### Scenario Framework and Interactive Viewer

A well-level scenario framework was implemented to translate the per-well SSM parameterization into site-wide spatial summaries of head change (Δh) under prescribed climate and forest management perturbations. For each well, the scenario head change relative to baseline was computed directly from the per-well SSM equation as:

$$\Delta{h = \left( {\beta_{1}\cdot P_{\mathit{eff},\mathit{sc}}-\beta_{2,\mathit{sc}}\cdot\mathit{PET}_{\mathit{sc}}-\beta_{3}\cdot h_{\mathit{disp}}} \right)}-\left( {\beta_{1}\cdot P_{\mathit{eff},0}-\beta_{2}\cdot\mathit{PET}_{0}-\beta_{3}\cdot h_{\mathit{disp}}} \right)$$

where P_eff applies the relevant canopy interception factor at forest wells (C4 and C5; 24% under the Corsican pine baseline following Freeman (2008); 15% annual mean under broadleaf conversion following Komatsu et al. (2011); 12% under 50% thinning; 0% under full clearfell), and β₂,sc applies a scenario-specific multiplier at forest wells. For full clearfell, the multiplier is derived dynamically from the BACI-corrected Edge-tier post-felling β₂ ratio reported in Section 4.6.6 (Edge mean ratio minus Climate Control mean drift, plus 1.0). The Edge tier is used as a conservative upper bound: although Edge wells were not directly felled, they recorded the largest tier-mean β₂ increase of any near-felling tier, while the directly-felled Impact well showed a smaller ratio not statistically distinguishable from the Climate Control drift. Adopting the Edge ratio therefore yields a precautionary upper bound on canopy-removal-attributable β₂ change. The thinning multiplier is set as half the clearfell perturbation.

Under broadleaf conversion, β₂ is scaled seasonally with phenological windows: a leaf-on (May--October) multiplier applied above the Corsican pine baseline, and a leaf-off (November--April) multiplier applied below it, reflecting the seasonally asymmetric transpiration signature of deciduous canopy compared to the year-round pine. The two phenological multipliers are estimated from the BACI Edge-tier monthly β₂ profile under the assumption that broadleaf canopy approaches the leaf-off canopy state in winter and a moderate-transpiration state in summer. Canonical values and their derivation are presented in Section 4.9.6. The same clearfell multiplier is applied at both C4 and C5 forest wells; no felled C5 wells were available in the BACI design, so the C5 application represents extrapolation from the C4 near-felling signal rather than direct measurement.

The β₃·h_disp term is identical in the scenario and baseline expressions and cancels in the difference. Specific yield Sy does not appear in the equation because the fitted β coefficients already embed the aquifer storage response through the SSM fit to observed head data; the per-well WTF-derived specific yield values (Section 3.7.3) are retained as supplementary display information in the interactive scenario viewer, not as a divisor on Δh.

Six scenarios were evaluated: baseline; UKCP18 2050s (winter P +10%, summer P −15%, winter PET +5%, summer PET +20%, RCP8.5 central estimate for Wales, informed by the UKCP18 Regional 12 km ensemble of Met Office (2018) and the CHESS-SCAPE bias-corrected projections of Robinson et al., 2023); UKCP18 2080s (winter P +20%, summer P −30%, winter PET +10%, summer PET +35%, same sources); full clearfell; 50% thinning; and broadleaf conversion. Climate scenarios were evaluated per season, with the annual Δh reported as the 0.5-weighted mean of the winter and summer equilibrium responses.

The per-well Δh field was interpolated to a site-wide 50 m grid on the British National Grid (EPSG:27700) using Delaunay triangulation with linear barycentric weighting (scipy.interpolate.griddata, method=\"linear\"), masked to the rectangular sea-boundary extent; the resulting field is rendered in the interactive scenario viewer described below rather than as a static map. Two wells were excluded from the interpolation: CEH12 (bedrock-anchored, geologically distinct from the dune aquifer) and CEH15 (forest slack edge, transitional between Forest and Western Residual clusters). The hydraulic conductivity reported for the site (K = 6.0 m/day; Betson et al., 2002) is retained as directional context for the Darcy flow vectors shown in Figure 49 and does not enter the Δh calculation.

The accompanying interactive scenario viewer (Hollingham, 2026; scenario_viewer.html) renders the same per-well Δh field using inverse-distance-weighted interpolation (power 1, eight nearest neighbours) for responsiveness under slider-driven re-interpolation, and offers a complementary depth-below-surface view obtained by subtracting the IDW-interpolated head field from the high-resolution DEM on a per-cell basis and masking inter-dune ridge cells (where the DEM exceeds the well-plane IDW elevation by more than 1.0 m) to confine the visualization to hydrologically meaningful slack positions. The viewer and the static figures therefore report matching per-well Δh values but use distinct interpolation methods and present complementary quantities at the grid-rendering stage.

A two-dimensional finite-difference PDE model was initially implemented during development as an alternative spatial framework, using the Helmholtz form of the steady-state groundwater flow equation in level form (Bear, 1972; Freeze and Cherry, 1979):

$$\nabla\cdot\left( {T\cdot\nabla h} \right)-\beta_{3}\cdot{h = -}\left( {\beta_{1}\cdot P_{\mathit{eff}}-\beta_{2}\cdot\mathit{PET}} \right)$$

The PDE works in level form rather than the displacement formulation of the SSM (Section 3.4) because it solves directly for the equilibrium head field h(x, y) under Dirichlet sea-boundary conditions, where the constant datum offset would be absorbed into the boundary specification. With transmissivity T = K·b (K = 6.0 m/day after Betson et al., 2002; b IDW-interpolated from four borehole constraints after Bristow, 2003), Dirichlet head conditions at sea boundaries, and implicit Neumann no-flow at the ridge, the sparse linear system of approximately 4,200 equations was solved using scipy.sparse.linalg.spsolve (Virtanen et al., 2020). The solver produced physically plausible baseline head surfaces and Darcy flux fields, but forest management scenarios evaluated through the PDE produced near-zero site-wide differences (mean Δh = −0.003 to −0.008 m for full clearfell and thinning). This reflects three structural limitations: the β coefficient changes affect only the forest wells (C4 and C5), which when IDW-interpolated to the grid are diluted by the surrounding clusters; the weak drainage feedback at C4 means a moderate source term change produces only a small equilibrium head change; and the elevated boundary condition at the ridge margin, where the C4 wells occupy the highest topographic positions in the dune system, is not parameterized in the source terms. Combined with the sparse constraints on K (a single tracer test) and b (four borehole logs across 700 ha), the PDE approach was judged to overclaim relative to the data available, echoing the calibration difficulties that constrained Betson et al.\'s (2002) MODFLOW model at this site. The well-level IDW framework described above was therefore adopted as the primary spatial analysis, on the basis that it retains the physical content that the SSM parameterization supports without claiming spatial flow dynamics the monitoring data cannot constrain.

All scenario outputs are provided through a self-contained interactive viewer allowing site-wide and cluster-level Δh responses to be explored under any combination of the six defined scenarios and their underlying parameter sliders (scenario_viewer.html; available at [*https://newbroman.github.io/Newborough_Hydrology/scenario_viewer.html*](https://newbroman.github.io/Newborough_Hydrology/scenario_viewer.html)).

*The spatial groundwater analysis and scenario mapping are implemented in 19_spatial_groundwater.py. Publication-quality spatial figures are produced by 20_spatial_figures.py. The forestry scenario equilibrium framework and the broadleaf seasonal β₂ derivation are implemented in 21_forestry_scenarios.py.*

## Computational Implementation

### []{#anchor-31}Data Pre-processing and Time-Series Management 

All data pre-processing, statistical modelling, and spatial mapping were executed within a Python programming environment. Time-series data manipulation, interpolation of missing temporal records, and standardization were performed using the pandas and NumPy libraries.

*Data preparation including quality control, gap-filling and the canonical geometry derivation is implemented in 01_data_prep.py; baseline climate figures and network summary statistics are produced by 00_climate_summary.py.*

### Statistical and Predictive Modelling 

The core parameterization of the aquifer mechanics was executed using the statsmodels module. For the continuous state-space modelling (Section 3.4), the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) algorithm was constrained to fit through the origin (omitting the intercept constant) to enforce physical mass balance. Conversely, seasonal prediction equations predicting peak flood and summer drought minima (Section 3.6.2) used unconstrained OLS regressions. The statsmodels architecture was further used to extract 95% confidence intervals and p-values for all SSM and ANCOVA coefficients, including the era-specific β₃ regressions of Section 3.5.3 and the ANCOVA-BACI β coefficients of Section 3.5.4. Iterative forecasting metrics, including the Nash--Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), were computed via NumPy array operations to benchmark the state-space model against traditional regression approaches (Section 3.4.2).

*State-space model fitting and the shared SSM utility functions used by all downstream scripts are implemented in utils/model_utils.py. Shared pipeline constants --- including DRAINAGE_DATUM, HEADLINE_LAG, FOREST_INTERCEPTION, and the canonical cluster labels and colours --- are defined in utils/config.py.*

### Geospatial Processing and Cartographic Visualization 

The integration of the topographical data with the monitoring network was managed through a dedicated spatial stack. GeoPandas and Fiona were used to parse external KML feature boundaries (e.g. the clearfell perimeter and hydrological boundaries) and standardize all spatial geometries to the British National Grid coordinate reference system (EPSG:27700).

The high-resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) was ingested and masked using the rasterio library. To visualize the localized dune topography effectively, the DEM arrays were rendered using a dual-slope normalization technique (TwoSlopeNorm) provided by matplotlib, anchoring the visual transition at specific elevation thresholds to highlight critical hydrological features. Contextual basemaps were fetched via contextily when necessary, and the label placement and occlusion avoidance was handled using the adjustText library.

*Spatial coefficient mapping and the SSM spatial fits (Section 3.4.3) are implemented in 07_spatial_coefficients.py. Shared geospatial utilities used across the spatial analyses are in utils/paths.py (output path conventions) and utils/map_utils.py (map rendering helpers).*

## []{#anchor-32}**Data requirements and Replicability**

****A deliberate objective of this study was to demonstrate the hydrological insight achievable from minimal, low-cost monitoring infrastructure. All primary data inputs consist of manual dipwell measurements, recorded with a standard electrical contact meter or tape measure, and publicly available monthly climate summaries from the Met Office historic station dataset. No specialist survey equipment, telemetry, or laboratory analysis was required. Potential evapotranspiration was estimated using the Thornthwaite and Mather (1957) method specifically because it requires only mean monthly air temperature --- a variable recorded at every Met Office station and at the majority of automatic weather stations worldwide. Methods requiring wind speed, humidity, or radiation data were deliberately avoided as these would limit replicability to sites with more comprehensive climate instrumentation.****

The analytical framework presented here could be deployed at any comparable lowland wetland, dune slack, or shallow unconfined aquifer system with a dipwell network and access to a nearby climate station. The principal constraint on analysis quality is record length rather than measurement sophistication; the state-space modelling and BACI analyses both benefit substantially from the long baseline available here, but meaningful cluster separation and mechanistic coefficient estimation are likely achievable with records of eight to ten years or more.
